stories.headline: Debt trap looms large over A.P. weavers
stories.deck: The weaving sector once sustained by handloom cooperative societies across Andhra Pradesh is currently reeling under mounting dues, dwindling orders and disappearing livelihoods, Nellore Sravani reports, as many societies are becoming dormant due to non-payment of dues on the part of the State government
stories.bodyText:
At 6 a.m., when most homes in Angara, a village in Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district, are still asleep, the looms in Balla Koteswara Rao and Balla Janaki’s cramped room are already at work. For the sexagenarian couple, a day means over 13 hours of work, putting in effort to weave one saree to barely save up ₹250 to ₹300 after expenses. Their labour keeps the loom moving back and forth, but delayed government payments keep them constrained to just meet ends.
“We manage to weave one saree in a day. After setting aside expenses for warps and wefts, we are left with ₹250 or ₹300 a day,” Janaki says, questioning how this is sufficient to run a family.
Pointing out the primary reason for their ordeal, Koteswara Rao says that the Andhra Pradesh State Handloom Weavers’ Co-operative Society Ltd. (APCO) failed to pay wages to the weavers. “For more than a year, we did not receive wages on time. If we furnish a saree today, we would get payment for the same after one or two months,” Koteswara Rao, in his late 60s, says.
According to the National Federation of Handlooms and Handicrafts (NFHH), which has been working with handloom weavers in the State since 1988, the State government is yet to pay ₹265.09 crore, an amount which has been pending since 2016, to APCO and handloom societies.
The weaving sector once sustained by cooperative societies across Andhra Pradesh, particularly in East and West Godavari and B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema districts, is currently reeling under mounting dues, dwindling orders and disappearing livelihoods.
Dwindling numbers
Andhra Pradesh is one of the major handlooms weaving regions in the country, unique for cotton and silk products including Ponduru, Uppada, Pedana, Mangalagiri, Venkatagiri, Dharmavaram, Chirala, Madanapalle, Madhavaram, among others.
According to the 4th All India Handloom Census 2019-2020, the State has 1,27,662 weavers and 49,785 allied workers. According to the Department of Handlooms, the State has around 415 cooperative societies, out of which only 200 are active, says Macherla Mohan Rao, president of the NFHH. The number of weavers, too, has come down to around 95,000, he says.
Formed with an objective of protecting the welfare of traditional artisans and preventing their exploitation at the hands of master weavers by providing continuous livelihood opportunities for them, handloom cooperative societies are organisations where weavers join hands for shared goals. The societies provide raw materials to their members, market the produce and ensure fair wages. The government also offered targeted benefits to society members to discourage weavers from seeking work from a master weaver.
However, the weavers in the Polavaram district attribute the collapse of the handloom cooperative societies in the State to the cessation of payments to be made by the government to these societies under the schemes of ‘Paavala Vaddi’ and Thrift Fund, and in the form of subsidies on raw materials, especially yarn.
The Polavaram cooperative society, set up in 1944, is one of the 36 cooperative societies of the composite district of Krishna and also one of the oldest in the State, which saw mushrooming of such societies in the years 1942-43.
According to the 2011 Census, the Polavaram village had a population of 3,345 individuals and 1,022 families. Out of these, around 700 families derived their livelihood from weaving. Most of them were members of the Polavaram Weavers’ Cooperative Production and Sale Society Ltd.
Today, the number of weavers working for the society stands at 215. Some of them left to work under master weavers and some others left for other professions, including agricultural work, even if it means more work and less pay, says K. Vasu, the society’s manager.
“It was to eliminate the middlemen and master weavers that such societies were formed. But today, the whole purpose is defeated, and we have gone back to living in the pre-Independence era,” Vasu says.
For one, Devi Vijayambika Weavers’ Cooperative Production And Sale Society Ltd., located in Pedana, has almost wound up its operations due to financial constraints. A small society, it once had around 30 weavers working, and now there are five left.
Chinta Rao, now in his 60s, was one of the last people from this society to start working for a master weaver. “What other choice did I have? All the benefits that we enjoyed once as society members have been taken away from us,” he says, adding that the manager of the society resigned a few years back.
Chinta Rao used to get financial support from both the Union and State governments in the form of yarn subsidy, thrift fund and also marketing incentives. Now, since most of these have been discontinued, he shifted to working for a master weaver.
What befell the handloom societies?
The issue dates back to the year 2018, when the then TDP government, months before the 2019 Assembly election, made a slew of promises to woo the weaver community in the region. During a programme in Chirala on August 7, 2018, then Chief Minister N. Chandrababu Naidu announced that the special rebate on handloom products, offered by the government to attract more customers and also give an edge to traditional weavers in a competitive market, will be increased from 20% to 30%. A Government Order, G.O. MS. No. 51, was issued in February, 2019, ordering for the enhancement.
Following this, societies began selling their produce directly to customers at a rate lower than the cost of production, hoping that the government would reimburse for the discounted rate. “We were given hopes. We gave away all our products at 30% less than the selling price,” says Chinta Rao.
Things turned upside down for the weavers when the government changed as Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy formed the Cabinet after winning the 2019 Assembly poll. “YSRCP leader Y. S. Jagan Mohan Reddy, who assumed the charge as the Chief Minister, did not care about the pending dues, but announced new welfare schemes like Nethanna Nestham, which did not help us much,” he adds.
Additionally, another GO was issued in February 2019, ordering for enhancement of the contribution made by the State government towards the Thrift Fund from the then existing 8% to 16%. But that also never happened. Mohan Rao says that while weavers are contributing to the Thrift Fund, the government stopped contributing its share from 2019. The implementation was patchy before too, he says.
Then, on March 8, 2019, the TDP government issued another GO, G.O. Ms. No. 55, ordering for enhancement of yarn subsidy from 20% to 40% on purchase of yarn, dyes and chemicals from National Handloom Development Corporation (NHDC) and APCO.
None of these was implemented after the YSRCP government came. “While the handloom sector in the State is facing the worst crisis today, a similar situation unfolded in 1995 when N. Chandrababu Naidu was the Chief Minister. Then, too, huge payments were pending to societies,” Mohan Rao recalls.
One of the reasons that many societies lie dormant today is because of non-payment of dues, he says.
A society borrows cash credits from District Cooperative Central Banks (DCCBs) for procuring raw materials to be supplied to its member weavers. The collective bunch of handwoven products produced by the weavers of a society are then sold to private traders or is procured by the APCO, which makes the payment after selling the products in markets. The amount received from the APCO and the government is then used to repay the loans taken from the banks.
Awaiting payments from govt.
According to the managers and weavers, APCO has never made payments on time because they were also waiting for payments from the government.
According to the data from the NFHH, APCO distributed products procured from societies to various government schools, but the government is yet to pay APCO for the same. The Social Welfare Department owes APCO ₹2.97 crore, the Tribal Welfare Department owes ₹20.33 crore, BC Welfare owes ₹9.99 crore, and the Department of Health, Medical and Family Welfare owes 12.59 crore. In total, APCO has to receive ₹90.53 crore from various government departments.
Since the apex body was not paid on time, it could not pay the societies on time. When payments were delayed by more than a year, the weavers bore the brunt.
Handloom weavers in Angara, a village in Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district, launched a relay hunger strike in October 2025 that went on for 16 days, demanding that payments be made immediately.
While Labour Minister Vasamsetti Subhash promised them that their grievances would be resolved, nothing has changed so far, the manager of a society in Dr. B.R. Ambedkar Konaseema district says on condition of anonymity.
Usually, banks give cash credits to a society at an interest rate of 12%. “Since 2018, due to non-payment of dues, whatever little we are earning by selling our products to traders is also going towards clearing the interest,” says the manager. The government owes ₹3 crore to this society, and the manager says they expended more than ₹70 lakh towards clearance of interest.
“There is no escape from the mounting debts. What use is the annual financial aid of ₹25,000, being distributed to weavers under the government’s Nethanna Sevalo scheme, when our debts are running into lakhs? We just want our money back,” the manager says.
For the Polavaram weavers’ society, the State government owes ₹52 lakh in total, says Vasu. “There was a time when we were making profits to the tune of ₹12 lakh, and after paying the wages, the remaining amount used to be distributed among the members as bonus,” he says, adding that while the bonus earlier used to be ₹10,000, it has now come down to ₹900.
Last year, the total sales at the society touched ₹1.19 crore, against the cost of production that stood at ₹1.07 crore. But the delayed payments have not had much impact on Krishna district societies. After earmarking 40% of the proceeds towards society’s reserves, the rest was distributed among 215 weavers in the form of a bonus, which would be ₹3,500 per weaver.
Meanwhile, the societies in Krishna district also sell their produce to private traders directly.
No elections since 2013
The cooperative societies were developed by weavers and for the welfare of weavers. But in Andhra Pradesh, elections to these societies have not been held since 2013. The five-year term of the body elected in 2013 ended in 2018. Since then, Handloom Development Officers have been made in charge of these societies.
When asked about this, Chief Special Secretary, Handlooms Department, R.P. Sisodia said the elections would be held after the conduct of the local body elections. There was no response to the question on the status of payments to the societies.

stories.headline: ‘It is unholy, It is illegal’: Iran President Pezeshkian denies nuclear bomb ambition
stories.deck: Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has reiterated the peaceful intent of the country's nuclear program, emphasizing that it is not designed for weapon development. He expressed Iran's willingness to cooperate with international inspections and reduce its stockpile of enriched uranium. Pezeshkian pointed to the US's preference for military action over diplomatic solutions as a key factor in…
stories.bodyText:
Iranian President 
Masoud Pezeshkian
 has ruled out any ambition to develop a nuclear weapon and said Tehran is ready to allow international inspectors to verify its nuclear programme, including measures to dilute its enriched uranium stockpile.
Speaking to Fox News on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York, Pezeshkian said Iran was prepared to accept international verification but insisted that the country’s nuclear programme was not aimed at developing a bomb.
“Not at all. Not at all. Our martyred, esteemed supreme leader had announced several times that from a religious decree, it is unholy. It is illegal,” Pezeshkian said.
Pezeshkian also said Iran was willing to reduce its enriched nuclear material and accept international monitoring.
“So that weapon's mass destruction. We said we’re willing to dilute them. It’s not a big deal. We are willing to submit ourselves to verification,” he told Fox News.
The comments come as Iran's nuclear programme remains under scrutiny from the International Atomic Energy Agency. The IAEA has said it has been unable to obtain information from Iran on the status of its declared nuclear material and facilities or conduct in-field verification at affected sites, leaving it unable to fully carry out its safeguards responsibilities.
The IAEA Board of Governors on September 9 also referred Iran's nuclear non-compliance issue to the United Nations Security Council, escalating the dispute over Tehran's safeguards obligations.
Pezeshkian also blamed the United States for the escalation, saying Washington chose military action instead of continuing negotiations.
“The problem is that America, instead of conducting dialogue, they descend into the arena by bombing us first, by blocking every pathway. They attacked us,” he said.
He reiterated that Iran's military response was defensive and said Tehran did not want to continue the conflict.
US President Donald Trump has maintained that preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon is a central US objective, while also saying that Washington and Tehran are continuing to communicate.
On September 22, Trump said he believed the two sides would eventually reach a settlement, but stressed that Iran could not be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon. Reuters

stories.headline: Asian Games 2026 India’s medallists: Full list of winners
stories.deck: Here’s the full list of Indian medallists at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games 2026 categorised by sport
stories.bodyText:
The 2026 Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games are underway in Japan. India is currently placed at the 15th spot on the medals’ table with seventeen medals. China is leading the table with 130 medals. Japan is second with 91 medals and Republic of Korea is third with 51 medals.
The Indian 4x400m mixed relay quartet of Vishal T.K., M.R. Poovamma, Manu T.S. and Vithya Ramraj earned a silver medal in the final at the Paloma Mizuho Stadium.
Seema Kumari, competing in her first Asiad, won a bronze medal in the 10,000m at the Asian Games, 16 years after Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut’s historic gold-silver double in 2010.
Manipur’s Naorem Roshibina Devi won her third consecutive Asian Games medal, clinching silver after losing to Zhang Xiaoyu in the women’s 60kg wushu final on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Jay Meena secured India’s first-ever soft tennis medal at the Asian Games, fetching a bronze after losing to Japan’s Takuya Kurosaka in the men’s singles semifinals. Star Indian weightlifter Mirabai Chanu completed her medal collection, winning a silver medal in the women’s 49kg event in the Asian Games.
Lakshya Sen and Ayush Shetty faltered against higher-ranked opponents as the Indian men’s team concluded with a bronze medal after losing 1-3 to their rivals, China, in the semifinals.
The Indian Women’s Cricket Team clinched a historic victory at the Karogi Athletic Park in Nisshin, Aichi. Facing off against Sri Lanka in a high-stakes final, the Women in Blue triumphed to secure India’s very first gold medal of the tournament.
Meanwhile, shooters have led the charge for India. The women’s skeet team, comprising Raiza Dhillon, Maheshwari Chauhan and Parinaaz Dhaliwal, won a bronze with a combined score of 331 here on September 23, 2026.
Experienced rifle shooter Elavenil Valarivan played a starring role in the country’s double-silver haul in the women’s 10m air rifle competition. Elavenil, one of India’s most accomplished rifle shooters, helped the country secure silver in the team event along with Sonam Maskar and Vidarsa Vinod. She then went on to add an individual silver.
For the men’s side, teenager Himanshu Dhillon produced a superb performance to win silver, while former world champion Rudrankksh Patil clinched bronze as India secured two individual podium finishes in the men’s 10m air rifle event. The two then teamed up with Parth Mane to win another silver in the team event, finishing just behind China.
After an impressive start in shooting, India also managed to script history in Mixed Martial Arts (MMA), with Suchika Tariyal winning the nation’s first-ever bronze medal for MMA at the Asian Games.
A contingent of 501 Indian athletes, comprising 267 men and 234 women, is competing across 36 disciplines in the 2026 edition. Apart from shooting, athletics and archery too are expected to add to the medal tally. India is also defending both the men’s and women’s titles in cricket and kabaddi.

stories.headline: ‘Jaldi kar, Panvel nikalna hai’: Comedy show turns ugly at an Ahmedabad university
stories.deck: During a comedy event at Nirma University, a student's remark led to a confrontation with a professor. The professor allegedly grabbed the student's collar and issued a threat in response. The National Students' Union of India demanded an apology from the professor and called for an impartial inquiry into the incident. The university has not yet publicly responded to these demands or commented on…
stories.bodyText:
AHMEDABAD: A student's alleged remark, "Jaldi kar, Panvel nikalna hai," during a comedy show at Nirma University in Ahmedabad has led to a controversy after a video purportedly showing a professor grabbing the student's collar went viral on social media.
The incident allegedly took place during 'Technofora 2026', a three-day event organised by students of the university's Institute of Technology from September 18 to 20.
What happened during the event
According to the claims surrounding the video, a professor and head of the electrical and instrumentation department was addressing students when the student shouted the remark, referring to a dialogue from the Bollywood film 'Golmaal'.
The professor then called the student on stage and allegedly grabbed him by the collar, as seen in the video.
The professor is also heard threatening the student in the video, saying, "I can go to any extent. The day you dare to insult any faculty member of the Nirma University campus, you are gone forever."
The video purportedly shows the incident during a stand-up comedy show featuring comedian Rajat Sood.
NSUI demands apology, inquiry
The Congress-affiliated National Students' Union of India (NSUI) has demanded an apology from the professor and an inquiry into the incident.
NSUI state vice president Vedant Tomar said, “The professor must apologise to the student and the university should conduct an impartial inquiry into the incident.”
Bhavik Solanki, national coordinator of the NSUI, claimed in a statement that the student was subjected to inappropriate behaviour and also demanded an apology from the professor and an inquiry.
The NSUI said it would hold a protest if its demands were not met.
University yet to respond
The private university did not respond to an email seeking its comment on the incident.
The circumstances leading to the confrontation, including the student's alleged remark and the professor's response, could not be independently verified.

stories.headline: Oil prices fall as markets look to Iran truce, but remain wary of attacks on oil facilities
stories.bodyText: Perth: Oil prices fell slightly on Friday as markets weighed the possibility of a truce between the US and Iran against the bombing of Saudi Arabia by Houthi rebels after a week of price spikes.Brent was down 74 cents, or 0.69%, to $105.85 a barrel at 0032 GMT, while West Texas Intermediate (WTI) was down 81 cents, or 0.86%, at $93.80 a barrel.The sluggish opening was a contrast to a week of volatility when oil prices rose to a one-week high on Thursday. Both contracts rose as much as 5%. Brent settled up 3.4% and WTI was 2.7% higher..Iran's president says it is up to US to choose if it wants to end Iran war.Brent notched its highest close since September 15. It was the first rise in days for WTI, which was down 13% over the prior six sessions and is down 6.42% for the week, compared with Brent’s 2.09% rise.US and Iranian negotiators in New York are exploring a phased path out of war that would involve Tehran reopening the Strait of Hormuz and Washington lifting its economic blockade of Iran, sources close to the talks said this week.“Diplomatic hopes are essentially helping oil prices weather the latest military strikes in the Middle East, with crude trading moderately softer despite the attacks,” said Tim Waterer, chief analyst at KCM Trade.Since the war began at the end of February, around a fifth of the world’s oil and gas shipments have been curtailed, pushing up prices by 50% in March alone while driving liquefied natural gas buyers to look further afield for new, stable supplies of the super-chilled fuel.On Thursday, Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian said it was up to the US to choose when the Iran war will end."It's America that must choose whether it wants to end this or not," Pezeshkian said, responding to a question in an interview aired on Thursday on Fox News.Saudi Arabia intercepted six ballistic missiles fired by Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis, thwarting attacks on the southern province of Taif and the Yanbu area on the Red Sea, the Saudi-led coalition in Yemen said.Ongoing attacks “serve as a clear reminder that critical oil assets remain firmly in the firing line,” Waterer said.Saudi Arabia is building up crude pumping volumes through its East-West Pipeline that runs to its Red Sea export hub of Yanbu, although crude tanker loadings have yet to resume, according to industry sources, satellite imagery and shipping data.

briefs.headline: Trump hosts Xi for state dinner as pomp masks tensions
briefs.deck: U.S. tech titans attended the banquet, including Tesla's Elon Musk, Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Sam Altman of OpenAI, underscoring that trade and AI were high on the agenda for Xi Jinping's visit
briefs.bodyText:
U.S. President Donald Trump hosted Chinese leader Xi Jinping for a lavish state dinner at the White House on Thursday (September 25, 2026), after a day of pomp and ceremony that masked deep tensions between the rival superpowers.
Numerous U.S. tech titans attended the banquet, including Tesla's Elon Musk, Apple's Tim Cook, Nvidia's Jensen Huang and Sam Altman of OpenAI, underscoring that trade and artificial intelligence were high on the agenda for Mr. Xi's visit.
Protesters gathered outside the White House as Mr. Trump and his wife Melania welcomed Mr. Xi and his wife Peng Liyuan for dinner, chanting slogans including "Xi Jinping is not welcome" and "Free Hong Kong," AFP reporters witnessed.
Earlier in the day, Mr. Trump proclaimed that he and Mr. Xi had made "tremendous strides" as he laid on pageantry including a military parade, a flyover and a tour of his new White House helipad.
"President Xi and I both understand that we represent different systems, but the ties between our people endure," Mr. Trump said at the dinner.
But Mr. Xi took a more restrained tone, calling for China and the United States to "coexist in peace" even as he laid down Beijing's red lines on AI, Taiwan and the Iran war.
He continued the theme in his dinner remarks, saying, "China and the United States must act as responsible major countries."
Bald eagle statue
Mr. Trump presented Mr. Xi with a gift of a custom-made statue of a bald eagle -- the national symbol of the United States. Guests dined on yellow squash veloute, sesame-crusted sea bass, and vanilla cremeux with White House honey ice cream.
The 80-year-old U.S. President guests to tour the building site of his new $400 million ballroom after the dinner, saying: "In honor of you, you'll be the first people to step foot on that."
While business was on the menu at the state dinner, expectations of any breakthroughs from Mr. Xi's visit are low.
One minor success -- the extension of a trade truce by two months until January -- was less than the two years that the Chinese had been hoping for.
Instead, the visit was more about spectacle than substance, with the pomp helping to smooth over the tensions that divide the world's two top economies.
A formal welcome on the White House South Lawn launched Thursday's (September 24, 2026) events, before Mr. Trump and Mr. Xi inspected a military parade on the newly paved-over Rose Garden.
American military jets -- including a B-2 bomber of the type that bombed Iranian nuclear facilities last year -- then staged a flyover as U.S. and Chinese flags flew over the West Wing.
As they began talks in the Oval Office, Mr. Trump joked that the Chinese had the friendliest press corps.
His comment came days after he barred outlets CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House -- although they returned on Thursday (September 24, 2026) after a court order.
'Great meeting'
Mr. Trump later walked Mr. Xi out to see the new helipad he had built at the White House and took the Chinese leader aboard his Marine One helicopter.
"We had a great meeting," Mr. Trump said, as the pair ignored questions on subjects including Iran, Taiwan, fentanyl trafficking and jailed Hong Kong pro-democracy media mogul Jimmy Lai.
But Xi's comments were often pointed
In his arrival remarks he said the two countries must ensure there is "no conflict and no confrontation" and said that AI must remain "always under human control."
Mr. Trump has in contrast played down warnings that AI could threaten humanity.
Later in the Oval, Mr. Xi urged Mr. Trump to show "prudence" and oppose independence for the flashpoint of Taiwan, the self-governing island that Beijing claims.
The Chinese leader -- whose country has reportedly shared intelligence with Tehran -- also urged Mr. Trump to end the Iran war "through negotiation as soon as possible."
Mr. Xi's visit wraps up on Friday (September 25, 2026) as the presidential couple pays a visit to the U.S. National Archives, home to the Declaration of Independence, which marks its 250th anniversary this year.

briefs.headline: CMRL-Exalogic payoff case raises legal, political challenges to govt., investigating agencies
briefs.deck: The allegation that Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, and other politicians too had received money from CMRL surfaced on Thursday as the State government was all set to issue a notification on the formation of a special investigation team to probe the findings of the ED against former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter T.…
briefs.bodyText:
The controversies involving Cochin Minerals and Rutile Limited (CMRL), the firm facing allegations of money laundering involving former Chief Minister Pinarayi Vijayan, his daughter T. Veena, and her husband P.A. Mohamed Riyas in the Exalogic pay-off case, have given way to legal and political challenges to the State government as well as investigating agencies.
The allegation that Chief Minister V.D. Satheesan, Home Minister Ramesh Chennithala, Health Minister K. Muraleedharan, and other politicians too had received money from the CMRL surfaced on Thursday as the State government was all set to issue a notification on the formation of a special investigation team to probe the findings of the Directorate of Enforcement against the three in the money laundering case.
Shone George, the BJP leader who released the reported pay-off list on Thursday, alleged that the government soft-pedalled Mr. Vijayan’s case and opted for a preliminary investigation rather than booking an FIR, as their names were also on the list of those who received funds from the company.
While the allegation against Mr. Satheesan and others was that they received money from the CMRL, Mr. Vijayan and his family members were accused of laundering the money using the alleged business deals of Exalogic, the now-defunct firm of Ms. Veena, with the CMRL. The names of the Chief Minister and others were reportedly mentioned in a diary seized from the officials of the CMRL. However, the ED had written to the State government that it had seized a diary from Ms. Veena in which the alleged details of hawala transactions were found included in her handwriting.
Though the ED had sought the probe on the ground that it had reportedly found the commission of a cognisable offence, legal options are limited for the agency to fix a time-frame for the State police to complete the preliminary investigation or force the registration of an FIR in the case.
The Keralam government is treading cautiously in the case involving the ED and the CPI(M) leaders considering its political ramifications, especially when the Congress had been complaining that the Union government was misusing investigating agencies for targeting Opposition parties.
The ED’s letter to the State police can be treated only as the sharing of information under Section 66 (2) of the Prevention of Money Laundering Act on a cognisable offence, which the agency stumbled upon during the course of its investigation. The police can drop the case and decide not to register an FIR if it could not find the commission of any cognisable offences as alleged by the ED, legal sources indicated.
However, there exists the legal possibility of a third party approaching the High Court seeking directives to the police for an effective probe and to register an FIR, as in the Tamil Nadu cash-for-jobs scam case (K. Athinarayanan vs The State of Tamil Nadu), though the decision of the High Court is under challenge before the Supreme Court, sources indicated.
The ED may require an FIR from the State police to take its probe against the CPI(M) leaders further in the event of an unfavourable verdict from the Delhi High Court in the CMRL’s petition challenging the Serious Fraud Investigation Office (SFIO) investigation in the pay-off case.
An order quashing the SFIO investigation will lead to the natural death of the ED’s case as the agency had used the final complaint of the SFIO to initiate its probe in the money laundering case. The case under the Prevention of Money Laundering Act can sustain only on the legal premises that the money, which is the proceeds of a crime, was laundered by the accused. Once the agency fails to prove the crime, the predicate offence, the money laundering case too will go, the sources indicated.
The Delhi High Court is likely to consider the CMRL’s petition on October 13.

briefs.headline: Zones of worry: Lives on the boil on forest fringes in Keralam after new ESA notification
briefs.deck: Keralam is once again witnessing a heated debate over the inclusion of some of its villages in the Western Ghats region in the Ecologically Sensitive Areas. Hiran Unnikrishnan and Sandeep Vellaram meet the stakeholders, including the settlers of the region and conservationists, to understand their concerns
briefs.bodyText:
It is barely noon, but dark clouds have already gathered over Randattumoonni, a hill hamlet deep inside Melukavu in the eastern high ranges of Kottayam. A cool breeze sweeps across the slopes before rain suddenly comes down in sheets, plunging the settlement into near darkness.
“It used to be even darker here when it rained,” recollects Tashkent Paikada, a settler farmer.
For those like Tashkent, these hills are not an untouched wilderness but a landscape shaped by generations of farming and settlement.
They fear that the proposed Ecologically Sensitive Area (ESA) notification for Western Ghats villages will uproot them from their lives, which were built by fighting inclement weather and marauding wildlife.
The seventh draft notification, the latest one in the series, issued on July 27, proposes to bring 9,993.7 sq km across 131 villages in Keralam under the ESA regime. Of this, 9,107 sq km is forest and 8,86.7 sq km is non-forest area. The deadline for filing objections was September 25.
Though the draft notification prohibits mining, quarrying and sand mining in the notified areas, there are no restrictions on the repair, extension or renovation of existing residential houses or on changes in ownership.
But in the high ranges, the notification has once again stirred fears about the impact of the classification on land, agriculture and everyday life.
Tashkent remembers the uncertainty that followed the earlier proposals.
“After 2013, people started cutting down trees as they feared they would not be able to use their land later. Farmlands were abandoned, and land prices fell. Apprehensions about the notification have done more damage here than anything else,” he says.
A landscape built by migration
The history of these settlements in the ghats region goes back to several generations.
The erstwhile Travancore administration’s Grow More Food campaign in the early 1940s encouraged migration to the high ranges. Families moved into the hills for farming. Over time, human habitations emerged and transformed large swathes of the mountains into agricultural landscapes.
Joseph Thomas, 85, a farmer from Udayagiri, near Kattappana, in Idukki has spent about six decades farming in the high ranges. His parents migrated from Kottayam to Idukki nearly 80 years ago.
For him, the present debate is not simply about environmental regulation but about the future of communities that have lived here for generations.
“If such regulations are brought in, people will eventually be forced to leave their land,” he fears.
Idukki, where 51 villages figure in the latest draft, has emerged as the epicentre of protests as during the times of the Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel report. All the grama sabhas passed resolutions urging the Union and the State governments to exclude their villages from the regime.
Melukavu panchayat president Bincy Tomy says the issue has already affected access to loans and land transactions. It has also impacted the marriage prospects of youngsters of the region, she points out.
Anil Sebastian, president of the Rubber Producers’ Society at Edamaruku in Kottayam, questions the ecological rationale for including Melukavu in ESA. The nearest forests, he says, are about 30 km to the north and 50 km to the south.
Church in the forefront
The Idukki Diocese of the Syro-Malabar Church has been at the forefront of the anti-ESA agitation since 2013. The High Range Samrakshana Samithy, under the patronage of the diocese, organised a series of protests across the high ranges. The Church continues to argue that human settlements and agricultural land should be kept outside the ESA.
“Human habitations and farmlands shall be fully excluded. Designating 51 villages as ESAs will disrupt normal life across the district. The Church supports the protests as the issue threatens the survival of the local population,” says Fr. Jins Karakkatt, director of the Idukki Diocese Media Commission.
The present anxiety is rooted in a decade-old debate over how the Western Ghats should be protected.
The concerns extend beyond the Church and its affiliates.
Alex Ozhukayil, chairperson of the Kerala Independent Farmers Association, sees the ESA proposal as creating two categories of residents, those who live in the ESAs and outside.
“The inclusion of a holding in the
The issue also reshaped district politics. In the 2014 Lok Sabha election, Joyce George, legal adviser to the Samithy and a Left Democratic Front(LDF)-backed Independent, won the Idukki seat, which was long considered a Congress citadel.
From Gadgil to Kasturirangan
The root of the dispute lies in the Madhav Gadgil-led Western Ghats Ecology Expert Panel report, which proposed a comprehensive zonation of the ghats based on ecological sensitivity.
In the high ranges, however, the report generated fears that agriculture and development would be restricted and that existing settlements could eventually face displacement.
Later, the Centre appointed a High-Level Working Group (HLWG) led by K. Kasturirangan to review the Gadgil recommendations. The HLWG, according to environmentalists, watered down the restrictions.
The first draft notification, based on the HLWG report and issued on March 10, 2014, proposed 123 revenue villages in Keralam, mainly in Idukki and Wayanad, as ESAs. But protests prevented the final notification from being issued, and six more draft notifications followed without resolving the dispute.
Subsequently, the State government-appointed Oommen V. Oommen committee recommended that inhabited areas, plantations and agricultural lands be excluded from the ESA through physical verification and field surveys. It also proposed re-fixing the ecologically sensitive areas using cadastral maps approved by the Kerala State Biodiversity Board. Those recommendations became the basis of Keralam’s position in subsequent negotiations with the Centre.
The arguments from conservationists are markedly different from those heard in the high range settlements.
N. Badusha, president of the Wayanad Prakruthi Samrakshana Samithy, says some interest groups are stoking unnecessary fears with ulterior motives.
“The apprehensions that there will be restrictions on building houses and digging wells in the ESAs are baseless political propaganda pushed by vested interest groups,” he says.
“We have a host of laws, including the Forest Act and the Wildlife Protection Act, to protect forests. So it is pointless to classify forest areas as ESAs to protect forests,” Badusha adds.
V.S. Vijayan, a member of the Gadgil panel, says the panel was misunderstood in the high ranges.
“The report only recommended a shift to organic farming. It never opposed farming. It opposed the pollution of water resources through chemical pesticides and called for non-polluting industries. There were no restrictions on local infrastructure development,” he says.
Vijayan says the panel’s approach was to give local communities a decisive role in determining how development should proceed in ecologically sensitive landscapes rather than impose a blanket ban on local activity.
Oommen also feels that the latest proposal is far removed from the version feared by high range residents.
“The latest draft notification has excluded farmlands and plantations from the ESAs. What is the interest of the high range communities in opposing the protection of fragile rocky land that is not owned by them?” he wonders.
Govt. seeks smaller ESAs
The State government will reiterate that its ESAs shall be limited to 8,590.69 sq km across 98 villages, excluding human habitations and agricultural areas. It wants the ecologically sensitive areas to be confined to forests and leased forest plantations. The demand also reflects a position taken by successive State governments, cutting across the political divide.
The State further argues that inhabited and cultivated landscapes should not be treated in the same manner as forests and other ecologically fragile areas. For residents, the distinction is critical because their houses, farms and livelihoods are embedded in the same landscape that conservation policy seeks to protect.
Residents and farmers’ organisations fear that an ESA designation could restrict them from using or developing their land. However, conservationists and those involved in framing the proposals argue that the notification is primarily intended to regulate activities that can damage fragile ecosystems.
For conservationists, the central issue is whether human activity in the Western Ghats can continue without weakening ecological safeguards. And that disagreement has been simmering for more than a decade of committees, consultations and draft notifications.
The farmers’ organisations have also linked the ESA debate to the Western Ghats’ UNESCO World Heritage status.
Mathew Varghese, State vice-president of the All India Kisan Sabha, the Communist Party of India’s (CPI) farmers’ wing, has demanded that the Western Ghats be excluded from the UNESCO World Heritage Site status, which demands more stringent conservation efforts.
“However, the UNESCO guidelines also say that if a project disrupts the livelihood or daily life of the local population, that area must be excluded,” he says.
Back in Randattumoonni, the hilly hamlet, the rain has begun to ease. Water rushes down the slopes towards the streams below, eventually joining the Meenachil river.
The same hills are viewed in two different ways: as a fragile ecological system that requires protection, and as a lived landscape of farms, homes and communities built over generations.
For people like Tashkent, the question is not whether the hills need protection. It is whether that ESA regime can accommodate the people who have made the hills their home.

briefs.headline: Rahul Gandhi a master of deception, allegations of vote theft lack evidence: BJP
briefs.deck: BJP leader Sudhanshu Trivedi asked whether there was any evidence that decisions by the Election Commission of India had not been taken unanimously
briefs.bodyText:
The Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) on Thursday (September 24, 2026) hit back at the Leader of the Opposition in the Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, calling him a “master of deception” with “zero political knowledge”, while responding to his allegations about “vote theft” and other election-related issues.
At a press conference, BJP MP and spokesperson Sudhanshu Trivedi said the Congress leader’s accusations lacked credible evidence. Countering Mr. Gandhi’s charge that every leader and party faced anti-incumbency except Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Home Minister Amit Shah, Mr. Trivedi said: “It is correct that anti-incumbency definitely is very consistent and strong against the Congress. The Congress has not returned to power in Tamil Nadu since 1967 and since 1977 in West Bengal, where there was a Communist government for 34 years... then Mamata Banerjee formed three governments.”
He said the Congress has not returned to power in Bihar since 1990; in Uttar Pradesh – the home State of the Gandhi family – there has been no Congress government since 1989; and since 1999, it has not formed a government in Odisha, where the BJD ruled continuously for 25 years. “After Rahul ji and Sonia ji came, the Congress is facing more anti-incumbency,” he said, citing the examples of Madhya Pradesh and Kerala.
“Definitely, during the era when the Congress also had governments for a long period of time, there were no voter ID cards, booth capturing used to take place, ballot boxes were looted, bullets were fired... in Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, there was hardly an election when some people were not killed and injured. Even then, anti-incumbency did not work against the Congress,” said Mr. Trivedi.
He alleged that the Congress had now been struggling to return to power as elections had become more transparent, with the process monitored through CCTV cameras, Central paramilitary forces deployed instead of local police, and an independent media and judiciary.
“In reality, today anti-incumbency for the Congress and the Gandhi family has become so strong that they cannot win their own seat without the help of their ally,” he said, alleging that Mr. Gandhi and Congress leader Priyanka Gandhi Vadra won Kerala’s Wayanad seat with the Muslim League’s support, and Amethi and Rae Bareli seats in Uttar Pradesh with the help of the Samajwadi Party.
Questioning the basis of a news report about communications between the Chief Election Commissioner and the two Election Commissioners, Mr. Trivedi asked whether there was any evidence that any decision in the Election Commission of India had not been taken unanimously.
He said the Special Intensive Revision process is authorised under the Representation of the People Act, arguing that voter lists needed proper verification to determine voter eligibility, particularly in areas impacted by “demographic change”. He also questioned whether an 18-year-old without any family records or documents should be allowed to become a voter without verification.
“In the 2024 Lok Sabha polls, the Congress got its biggest victory from Assam’s Dhubri seat, where the party’s Rakibul Hasan won by 10.25 lakh votes,” he said, stating that Dhubri had undergone major demographic changes over the past 20-25 years.

briefs.headline: 12 years of ‘Make in India’ in 12 metrics — Low and patchy impact on growth, employment & global share
briefs.deck: While recent incentive schemes by the government have seen some success, those gains are limited to a handful of sectors
briefs.bodyText:
Twelve years on from the launch of the Make in India campaign on September 25, 2014, a look at 12 metrics spanning growth, investment, employment, and exports shows that the manufacturing sector’s share in India’s economic growth, employment, and global exports has remained largely the same since then.
While recent incentive schemes by the government have seen some success, those gains are limited to a handful of sectors.
While launching the campaign, Prime Minister Narendra Modi said that “industrialists don’t come due to some fancy incentive scheme” but instead need a “development and growth-oriented environment”.
The data over the last 12 years show that while the government’s incentive schemes are the ones that have met some success, other metrics that reflect a “development and growth-oriented environment” are underperforming.
No major boost to growth
The manufacturing sector has grown faster than the overall economy in five of the 12 years under consideration, based on the old series. Under the new series, it has outpaced overall growth in all three years (2023-24 to 2025-26) for which data is available, but that gap is shrinking fast.
The Index of Industrial Production data, which comes out once a month, is more stark. The manufacturing sector within the IIP outpaced the overall index’s growth in only three out of the 12 years, as per the old series of the index. The new series shows the manufacturing sector’s growth was the same as that of the overall index in 2023-24, but was slower in the next two years.
As far as the composition of the economy goes, the older series of Gross Value Added (GVA) data shows the manufacturing sector’s share in overall GVA is lower in 2025-26 than it was when Make in India was launched in 2014. The new series shows that the sector’s share has increased marginally from 14.6% in 2022-23 to 15.6% in 2025-26.
Rising exports, flat share
India saw the value of its non-petroleum goods exports grow 53% to $388.3 billion in 2025-26 from $253.5 billion the year the Make in India campaign was launched. However, the data also shows that non-petroleum goods exports grew more than 400% over the 12 years before this, albeit on a much smaller base.
However, the base effect only accounts for some of this growth disparity. Data from UNCTAD shows India’s share in global merchandise exports grew from around 0.8% in 2002 to 1.7% in 2013, where it remained even in 2025-26.
Tepid investment response
The gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) by the private sector — a measure of its spending on real asset creation — formed a lower share of GDP in 2023-24, the latest year for which the old series has data, than it did in 2014-15. The new series, too, shows that GFCF as a percentage of GDP has been falling since 2022-23.
The growth of FDI to the manufacturing sector has been slower than the growth in overall FDI in seven of the 12 years under consideration. Its share in overall FDI grew from nearly 48% in 2014-15 to 55% in 2025-26.
The RBI’s data on capacity utilisation, a measure of how intensively factories are being used, shows that this metric never has been slowly increasing over the last few years, but is still below the 80% mark that is considered the limit after which companies invest to create new capacity.
The RBI’s data further shows that bank credit to industry has been growing strong over the last few years, especially led by credit to micro, small, and medium enterprises. However, experts have pointed out that, in the absence of sustained rapid growth in output, this suggests that the loans are being taken to provide working capital rather than for fresh investments.
Impact of incentives
The government’s Production-Linked Incentive schemes have yielded some results. Launched across 2020 and 2021, the 14 schemes have resulted in a cumulative investment of Rs 2.4 lakh crore as of March 2026. However, the data also shows that this performance is highly concentrated.
The top five sectors — solar modules, pharmaceutical drugs, automobiles and their components, specialty steel, and large-scale electronics manufacturing — together account for nearly 83% of all the investment under these schemes.
Flat employment effect
The food products, large-scale electronics manufacturing, pharmaceutical drugs, automobiles and their components, and white goods sectors cumulatively accounted for more than 86% of the 8.5 lakh people employed under these schemes.
The government says three sectors — large-scale electronics manufacturing, IT hardware, and solar modules — have resulted in an additional 5.7 lakh of indirect employment.
Data sourced by CMIE from the Ministry of Labour and Employment shows that the total number of people employed in the manufacturing sector grew from 5.1 crore in 2016-17 to 5.3 crore in 2025-26. The manufacturing sector’s share in total employment was largely the same in 2025-26 as in a decade earlier.

briefs.headline: Trinamool symbol freeze row: Supreme Court asks EC adjudication timeline
briefs.deck: The EC had said that the interim order, passed under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, would be in operation during the current byelections and will continue till the final determination of the dispute over the party
briefs.bodyText:
The Supreme Court on Thursday (September 24, 2026) signalled that it was unlikely to stay the Election Commission’s interim freeze on the All India Trinamool Congress’s (AITC) ‘flowers and grass’ party symbol.
However, the Court directed the poll body to set a reasonable timeline to adjudicate the leadership dispute between former West Bengal Chief Minister Mamata Banerjee and Ritabrata Banerjee, who leads the rival camp of legislators.
“Find out how much time you would need for the final adjudication of the dispute after giving parties due representation and for you to also apply your mind. We are not saying anything, but give a reasonable time, do not prolong,” Chief Justice of India Surya Kant told the Election Commission of India (EC) counsel, senior advocate Dama Seshadri Naidu.
The Court directed the EC to respond on Monday (September 28).
During the hearing, the Chief Justice referred to paragraph 39 of the EC’s interim order of September 17 which said that the freezing of the party symbol was necessary to place “both the rival groups on even keel and to protect their rights and interests”.
The EC had said that the interim order, passed under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968, would be in operation during the current byelections and will continue till the final determination of the dispute over the party.
The poll body had said neither groups would use the name of the party ‘All India Trinamool Congress’ simpliciter nor avail the reserved party symbol of ‘flowers and grass’. The EC had allotted new names and symbols to the two factions on September 18. The Mamata faction was allotted the name ‘Mamata All India Trinamool Congress’ and the symbol ‘football player’, while the Ritabrata group was allotted the name ‘Democratic Trinamool Congress’ with the symbol ‘envelope’.
Senior advocate Kapil Sibal and advocate Abhinav Singh submitted that the EC deliberately delayed proceedings on the party dispute and has wrongly passed an interim order pat in the middle of the schedule for the Nandigram Assembly byelection due on October 6.
“The intent behind this interim order is to leave me without a remedy… If you allow this order to continue, he [EC] will do it in the middle of every election. In another election, in another State, he will do the same,” Mr. Sibal submitted.
The Court expressed an objection to stay the interim order with Justice Joymalya Bagchi noting that symbols have already been allotted and candidates have filed nominations.
The Judge, however, said the court could look into whether the EC had recorded reasons extensively before passing the interim order of September 17.
“The solution in this case is to have the EC come to a final decision as quickly as possible,” the CJI observed
Justice Bagchi remarked, “We know what happened to the Shiv Sena due to delay.” Shiv Sena had also gone through a split which ultimately led to Uddhav Thackeray stepping down as Maharashtra Chief Minister and losing both party symbol and name to rival Eknat Shinde, the current Deputy Chief Minister.
Mr. Sibal said the Court should impose an October deadline on the EC to finally decide the dispute.
Senior advocates Mukul Rohatgi and Neeraj Kishan Kaul, appearing for the rival camp, said both rival parties need to cooperate for the EC to decide within a reasonable time. They said the flux has to be resolved in the spirit of democracy.
“They (EC) have other work also,” Mr. Rohatgi said. “We know what other work they have…” Mr. Sibal retorted.

briefs.headline: Opposition to move fresh notice for CEC’s removal; INDIA bloc mulls joint action
briefs.deck: New petition likely in both Houses of Parliament even as an earlier Rajya Sabha notice against Gyanesh Kumar remains pending; TMC urges swift and united Opposition response
briefs.bodyText:
Opposition parties will move a fresh notice seeking the removal of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar in both Houses of Parliament, even as a previous petition moved in the Rajya Sabha on April 24 is pending with Upper House Chairman C.P. Radhakrishnan.
The Opposition is also gearing up for joint action on the issue and could soon call for a meeting under the banner of the INDIA bloc. A senior Opposition leader said that a dialogue is going on among like-minded parties to discuss the modalities.
In view of the Cockroach Janta Party’s 48-hour ultimatum calling for Mr. Kumar’s resignation, the INDIA bloc is anxious not to be seen as latecomers on the issue. “The Opposition will certainly be moving, especially in light of the new revelations. Our earlier motion submitted on April 24, 2026, in the RS had nine specific charges. That motion is still pending. There will be more specific charges,” Congress general secretary (communications) Jairam Ramesh said.
The Trinamool Congress, which played a key role in the drafting of two previous petitions for Mr. Kumar’s removal, said a new petition should be moved at the earliest. “The TMC is very happy to play the role of a squirrel in the garden. The Opposition has to act unitedly and swiftly,” the party’s Rajya Sabha leader Derek O’Brien said.
First motion in March dismissed
It was on March 12 that the Opposition first moved a notice seeking Mr. Kumar’s removal. This notice was signed by 63 Rajya Sabha MPs and 130 Lok Sabha MPs.
It contained seven charges against the CEC, including that his appointment itself was “tainted, with the law governing his selection, the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act, 2023, facing a challenge in the Supreme Court. The Opposition also claimed that Mr. Kumar’s previous postings reflected “deep executive embeddedness”.
This notice was dismissed by the presiding officers of both Houses on April 7.
April notice still pending in Rajya Sabha
On April 24, the Opposition again moved a notice in the Rajya Sabha, signed by 73 Opposition members, this time with nine charges. The Leader of Opposition Mallikarjun Kharge and Congress Parliamentary Party chairperson Sonia Gandhi had not signed this notice.
The 13-page notice moved in April made several allegations: the EC’s “asymmetrical enforcement of the Model Code of Conduct”, citing the example of the EC ignoring a violation by Prime Minister Narendra Modi, who used the public broadcaster to denounce the Opposition in a recent address to the nation; the EC’s post on X directed against the Trinamool Congress ahead of polls in West Bengal; the poll body’s “institutional proximity” to the BJP, underlining an incident from Kerala where an official election document reportedly carried the seal of a BJP State unit; a spat between Mr. Kumar and a TMC delegation during a recent meeting at the EC headquarters in Delhi; “mass disenfranchisement” in West Bengal and Uttar Pradesh, and the ignoring of complaints filed by Opposition parties; and the “illegal abuse” of power through the transfer and posting of bureaucrats in Tamil Nadu, among other issues.

stories.headline: Bengaluru police issues guidelines to curb harassment, extortion by transgender persons
stories.deck: The move follows complaints about incidents at traffic signals, markets, bus, and railway stations, residential areas and function or ceremony venues.
stories.bodyText:
The Bengaluru City Police have issued guidelines to regulate complaints involving transgender persons allegedly harassing members of the public, obstructing traffic, aggressively soliciting money and engaging in other unlawful activities at public places.
The move follows complaints about incidents at traffic signals, markets, bus, and railway stations, residential areas and function or ceremony venues.
According to the guidelines, police have been instructed to verify the facts and circumstances of every complaint involving aggressive solicitation of money or alms, obstruction of public or vehicular traffic, threats, abusive behaviour, assault, or harassment, and take appropriate legal action in accordance with law.
Police stations have also been directed to identify locations within their jurisdictions from where repeated complaints are being received and arrange increased patrolling in such areas.
The police have been instructed to conduct regular meetings with members of the transgender community and create awareness against involvement in unlawful activities.
At the same time, the public will be informed about the immediate steps they can take when faced with harassment or violations of law.
The guidelines stress that while maintaining public order and ensuring smooth movement of traffic, the legal rights, dignity, and respect of transgender persons must be protected.
Police personnel have been specifically directed not to use derogatory, insulting or abusive language against transgender persons and to use respectful and non-discriminatory language while taking action against violations.
The Commissioner of Police has instructed all officers and personnel of Bengaluru City Police to strictly comply with the guidelines.
The public has also been advised not to panic during such incidents and to immediately contact the 112 emergency helpline, provide details of the incident and lodge a complaint at the nearest police station.
Rakshitha Mallikarjuna, a transwoman and social activist, acknowledged that there had been instances of transgender persons forcing members of the public to give money or behaving rudely. However, she argued that such a move could lead to excessive action against a community that is already marginalised, as it could create the impression that all transgender persons behave in the same way.
“We demand respect. Whatever money comes should be accepted without demanding or forcing. But why is seeking alms or any action by a transgender person being specifically notified against, while men, women, and even children are not warned against in a similar manner? Such measures may give the police the power to act against the community,” Rakshitha added.

stories.headline: Run, meet, repeat: Bengaluru’s running clubs are building communities
stories.deck: Run, meet, repeat: Bengaluru’s running clubs are building communities
stories.bodyText:
As dawn breaks over Bengaluru on weekends, running routes across the city become more than workout tracks. From the tree-lined stretches of Cubbon Park to the loops of Sankey Road and Kaikondrahalli Lake, runners gather not just to clock kilometres but to meet people. Somewhere between the first kilometre and the post-run coffee, strangers become familiar faces, regulars become friends, and running becomes a gateway to a wider social circle.
Run clubs: The bustling social circle in the city
Sidharth Yadav, founder of Stride Run Club, has watched Bengaluru’s running culture evolve over the years. He describes today’s clubs as the fourth generation since the 1960s — “but the first that’s inclusive and beginner-friendly.” Many clubs now pair running and walking with social activities such as pottery workshops and perfume-making sessions. For Arvind Srikanth, co-founder of 56 Run Club, fitness spaces are increasingly taking on the role once played by traditional social venues. “Now it’s about bringing people together where they can stay active, meet friends and have fun,” he says.
At HSR Run Club, what began as “a small group of people who just wanted to stay consistent” has grown into “a strong community where people support each other and celebrate milestones together,” says founder Deekshith Gowda.
Real community and real bonds form after the run — when people are winding down, chilling, and talking to each other.
Sidharth Yadav, Founder, Stride Run Club
For many younger runners, the appeal extends beyond fitness. Maninder Singh, co-founder of Main Mission (formerly Indiranagar Run Club), says people are looking for social spaces outside work and nightlife. “These runs are a social set up where you get to meet like-minded people. We organise social mixers for founders too,” he says. Sidharth adds that the typical age group at his club is 20 to 35. “Many are working professionals looking for new ways to socialise beyond the workplace, friend circles and dating apps,” he shares.
At 56 Run Club, millennials and Gen Z make up much of the 25 to 35 demographic, says Arvind. HSR Run Club, meanwhile, sees a broader mix. “We see people across different age groups, from Gen Z and millennials to Gen X. Everyone can run at their own pace and still be part of the same community,” says Deekshith.
Running has become a new weekend third space for people.
Arvind Srikanth, Co-Founder, 56 Run Club
For Sidharth, the café stop is an integral part of the experience. “Every run has to end at a café. That’s the rule we follow,” he says. He structures runs around icebreakers, mini-games and multiple pace groups, ensuring beginners aren’t left behind. “After the run, people meet over breakfast or a cup of coffee. And that’s where real community bonds form,” Sidharth adds. At 56 Run Club, Arvind says, “Many friendships and business connections have blossomed over the last two years.” Deekshith has seen a similar pattern at HSR Run Club. “Many people come for the run, but stay for the community.” Over time, he says, friendships have formed, business connections have developed and runners have found support systems beyond fitness.
Coach Neera Katwal of Champions says, “Running helps people stay more active, build confidence and develop a routine. And along the way, they make friends and find a community that keeps them coming back.”
A lot of runners end up hiring each other or working together. It’s a great way to spend a Sunday morning.
Maninder Singh, Co-Founder, Main Mission
“Bengaluru has a wonderful running culture,” says Neera. “The weather, particularly in the early mornings, makes it possible to run comfortably for much of the year.” Maninder, who has been running in the city for over two years, says, “It is a beautiful city to run in for sure... We would love better footpaths, better passages for runners and cyclists to go wherever they want to, but that progress has to happen over time.”
For Deekshith, infrastructure remains the biggest challenge. “Lack of proper footpaths, traffic at certain locations, and safety concerns can make running difficult. That’s why we encourage runners to choose safer routes, run in groups, and start early whenever possible,” he explains.
Running allows you to notice parts of the city that you would normally miss while driving.
Deekshith Gowda, Founder, HSR Run Club
“Every runner is different,” Neera says. Her group follows science-backed training, while celebrating incremental improvements. “We celebrate small improvements. I award my team T-shirts when they achieve milestones and personal best times.”
Deekshith says HSR Run Club focuses on creating a “non-judgmental environment”. “We make sure nobody gets left behind. Experienced runners often slow down, share tips, and encourage beginners throughout the run,” he adds.
“Life is not a sprint, it’s a marathon,” says Sidharth, an ISSA-certified coach. “You don’t have to give your 100%. Just pace yourself to 70% or 75%. That is the real secret to sustainability, in running and in life,” he adds. For Arvind, running is “more of a mental activity.” He says, “Running is a solo activity that can teach people to push past barriers they did not know they could clear.”
Many women trainees have improved their PCOD symptoms and fertility through running. Watching that change has been the most fulfilling part of running.
Neera Katwal, Coach, Champions
- Cubbon Park
- Lalbagh Botanical Garden
- Sankey Road
- Indiranagar–Domlur
- HSR Layout
- Agara Lake
- Kaikondrahalli Lake
- For beginners: Look for clubs that offer walkers, multiple pace groups and a no-pressure atmosphere
- For the social experience: Pick runs that include a café stop, breakfast, games or a post-run hangout
- Typical turnout: Around 30 to 50 runners at smaller clubs, with 100+ at larger weekend events
- What to expect: A warm-up, group run and cool-down, followed by time to socialise
- City-smart tip: Start early, run in groups and stick to familiar, safer routes

stories.headline: Soujanya case: Karnataka forms SIT headed by N. Shashikumar for fresh probe
stories.bodyText:
The State government has constituted a five-member Special Investigation Team (SIT) to conduct a fresh investigation into the 2012 Soujanya case registered at the Belthangady Police Station in Dakshina Kannada district and the FIR subsequently re-registered by the Central Bureau of Investigation (CBI).
Inspector-General of Police N. Shashikumar has been appointed as the SIT chief. The team includes Mangaluru City Police Commissioner C.H. Sudheer Kumar Reddy, State Intelligence Superintendent of Police Nisha James, Criminal Investigation Department (CID) Superintendent of Police Lokesh Jagalsar and Bengaluru Rural Additional Superintendent of Police Venkatesh Prasanna.
The government constituted the SIT following directions issued by the Supreme Court while hearing a special leave petition filed by Kusumavathi Gowda, mother of Soujanya. The court had directed the State government to complete the fresh investigation within three months and submit a report to the court, besides ordering constitution of an SIT for the purpose.
The SIT has been constituted with jurisdiction across Karnataka under the relevant provisions of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS), 2023, the order stated.
The government order stated that the SIT has been declared a police station for the territorial jurisdiction of Karnataka under Section 2(1)(u) of the BNSS, 2023. The investigating officers of the SIT have also been authorised to submit a police report before the competent court under Section 193 of the BNSS.
The SIT will function under the supervision of the Director-General and Inspector-General of Police, Karnataka.
The SIT has been given three months to complete the comprehensive investigation and submit its final investigation report to the competent court. After completion of the investigation, the DG&IGP will submit a report to the State government.

briefs.headline: Bhajan jamming:Bengaluru’s new weekend beat for kids
briefs.bodyText:
For some families in Bengaluru, a weekend outing meant less mall-hopping and more bhajan jamming. At Atta Galatta, parents and children gathered for a morning of devotional music, singing and dancing with storyteller Priya Subramanian and musician Anagha Karvir, creating a fun space for children to dance, participate and enjoy.
‘Kids also deserve a party’
Priya Subramanian wanted children to experience bhajans not as a formal concert, but as a celebration. “Kids also deserve to have a party — a satvik party where they can dance,” she says. Her bhajan jamming sessions combine devotional music and storytelling, drawing from Puranic tales that she feels can be both entertaining and child-friendly. “The stories introduce children to different deities in a more relatable way, focusing on the values and human ideas behind them rather than presenting gods as distant figures who simply teach strict lessons,” shares Priya.
We are exploring different ways of introducing music and stories from our culture. Growing up, we heard all tales of Gods. In Bengaluru, it is difficult to find places like this
Anagha, who came with her 2-year-old son
Priya sees potential for the format to become a regular family outing. “Parents have already asked if the sessions can be held more frequently. It can be a possible weekly dose of recharge or a monthly dose of recharge,” she says and hopes the sessions can bring grandparents into the experience, echoing their traditional role in passing down stories and wisdom. Her larger aim is to present that same warmth in a contemporary setting and help children connect with the spirit of Indian wisdom — particularly the idea of Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam, meaning the world is one family.
She has shown too much interest in rhythm and music from the very start. The blend of classical music and devotional songs made the session a good way to give her an early exposure

briefs.headline: Drought damages 62,985 hectares of onion crop in Karnataka; prices remain high
briefs.deck: While onions are being sold at ₹50-55 a kg in the wholesale market, retail prices range between ₹65 and ₹70 a kg
briefs.bodyText:
The price of onion, a staple in many kitchens, continues to remain high even as the Karnataka State Department of Horticulture (KSDH) has recorded onion crop losses in more than 60,000 hectares across 124 taluks due to severe drought.
While onions are being sold at ₹50-55 a kg in the wholesale market, retail prices range between ₹65 and ₹70 a kg.
A KSDH official said: “For the 2026-27 kharif season, onion sowing has been completed in 1,41,256 hectares against a target of 1,50,000 hectares. In the current year, 124 taluks have been declared drought-affected. A joint survey by KSDH and the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC) indicates that 62,985 hectares of onion crop have suffered damage exceeding 50%. An additional 53 taluks were declared drought-affected on September 22, and the extent of onion crop damage may increase. The joint survey process is currently under way in these 53 taluks.”
The official added: “The area covered under sowing in the kharif season is 94%, which is 6% lower than last year. Though the sowing percentage is good, we cannot expect a good yield, the obvious reason being the failure of rains. Onion prices may increase further due to crop failure and rising demand. Karnataka markets receive onions mainly from Maharashtra when there is no local yield in the State.”
Meanwhile, Chamarasa Malipatil, honorary president of the Karnataka Rajya Raitha Sangha (KRRS), said: “Onion is mainly cultivated in Vijayapura, Bagalkote and Chitradurga districts and in some parts of south Karnataka. Onion requires sufficient water for cultivation. In black soil, farmers need to irrigate it once in 20 days to retain moisture, while in red soil, water should be provided once every 10 days.”
Mr. Malipatil added: “For the past three years, onion prices were too low and farmers did not make profits. Prices were around ₹400-500 a quintal, or ₹10-15 a kg. As returns remained poor, some farmers in north Karnataka gave up onion cultivation altogether.”
Kharif yield important to stabilise the price
B.R. Raghu, Senior Scientist at the Indian Institute of Horticultural Research, Bengaluru, explained: “A major share of onion cultivation in Karnataka takes place during the kharif season because the crop can be grown well in rain-fed areas. Sowing begins in May and harvesting takes place in September and October. This year, arrivals may be delayed due to poor rainfall and crop failure. A good kharif harvest in Karnataka is crucial for onion price stability across India.”
“Of the total onion cultivation area in India, only about 30% is under the kharif crop, concentrated largely in Karnataka, parts of Madhya Pradesh and Nashik in Maharashtra. The remaining 70% falls under the rabi season and is cultivated in Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, parts of Karnataka, Odisha, Rajasthan and Bihar,” he said.
Mr. Raghu added that onions harvested during the rabi season in May are purchased by corporate firms and traders, stored, and released into the market during periods of high demand in October and November.
B. Ravi Shankar, of the Onion Merchants’ Association of Bengaluru, said that although the Union government released onion stocks through the Kanda Express scheme at ₹35 a kg to stabilise prices, the move had little impact on wholesale or retail prices in Karnataka. “They should have taken this step much before the price rise. Besides, Karnataka receives onions mainly from Maharashtra and the supply chain involves several stakeholders before the produce reaches consumers. Apart from weather conditions, storage, transportation and labour costs also play an important role in pushing up prices,” he said.
He added: “Prices are unlikely to come down until fresh onion stocks from the recent kharif crop in Karnataka reach the market. However, even that cannot be assured.”

briefs.headline: Karnataka CM, Dy. CM demand Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar’s resignation, seek fresh roll revision
briefs.bodyText:
Seeking the immediate resignation of Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) Gyanesh Kumar, Karnataka Chief Minister D.K. Shivakumar demanded that the ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls be withdrawn, followed by a fresh revision.
Mr. Shivakumar said the issue concerned the voting rights of every citizen and that it was not about any political party, arguing that the SIR had been conducted in a manner that could affect citizens. He said similar concerns had emerged in West Bengal, Bihar and other States. Karnataka, too, was now facing the same situation, he said, adding that he had sought more time from the Election Commission of India (ECI).
Questioning the functioning of the poll panel, Mr. Shivakumar pointed to differences among its members, with two Election Commissioners raising objections to major decisions, including changes to Form 6 and the ECI’s software. He said decisions should not be imposed when a majority did not agree with an opinion. “In such a situation, the Chief Election Commissioner should voluntarily resign on moral grounds,” he said.
Further questioning the manner in which Forms 6, 7 and 8 were being used during the revision, Mr. Shivakumar said the process needed wider scrutiny and argued that the issue should be discussed extensively, including in Parliament.
‘CEC not above the ECI’
Referring to the “vote chori” concerns raised by Leader of the Opposition Rahul Gandhi in the Mahadevapura and Aland Assembly constituencies, and allegations of duplicate voters in Haryana, Deputy Chief Minister G. Parameshwara sought an independent inquiry into the functioning of the ECI and demanded the removal of the CEC.
Dr. Parameshwara questioned whether the three-member constitutional body was functioning through collective decision-making when two of its members had raised objections to decisions being issued without their approval. “Has a three-member constitutional body been reduced to the will of one individual, Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar? He is first among equals, not above the Commission,” he said, arguing that the majority view could not be bypassed.
Pointing to objections over changes to Form 6, the Deputy Chief Minister said, “Mr. Kumar should not continue as CEC while questions remained over decisions taken under his leadership.“
