briefs.headline: Over 70 tree species among 1,128 marked for felling for Hebbal tunnel project in Bengaluru
briefs.deck: The species list includes Indian Kino, Big-leaf Mahogany, Beleric Myrobalan, Indian Jujube, Maple-leafed Bayur Tree, Paper Mulberry and Yellow Tabebuia, among others.
briefs.bodyText:
Over 70 species are among the 1,128 trees within the 2.2-km stretch scheduled to be felled for Bengaluru’s Hebbal short tunnel project. Apart from highlighting the massive biodiversity loss, experts argue that the move could substantially impact the microclimate, triggering a spike in temperature.
According to the Greater Bengaluru Authority (GBA) documents accessed by The Hindu, the species list includes:
- Queen’s crape myrtle
- Agati
- Yellow Tabebuia
- Mysore fig
- Big-leaf Mahogany
- Pongam tree
- Paper Mulberry
- Indian Kino
- Beleric Myrobalan
- Indian Jujube
The species diversity numbers could be much higher as the GBA is yet to upload the filtered list for the public to review and file objections.
While the initial number of trees to be felled was 1,400, GBA officials said a few hundred were decided to be retained as they were not in the tunnel’s alignment.
Impact on climate
R. Ganesan, Adjunct Fellow, ATREE, explained that such a large number of species within a 2-km stretch, particularly in an urban landscape, is not very common, although not unusual.
“In a forest setup, it is common to have a large number of species in a small area, but in a metropolitan area like Bengaluru, it highlights years of green space retention. The Hebbal area has already seen massive environmental destruction in the past few years; this move will directly impact the temperature,” he said.
A.N. Yellappa Reddy, former forest secretary, explained that felling over 1,000 trees will destroy several habitats and oxygen banks, besides impacting underground water levels.
“With such a massive destruction within a small area, the temperature will go up by at least two degrees and create heat islands, and that doesn’t mean that heat will go up in only that area. As a ripple effect, the temperature in another 2-km radius will go up,” he explained. “Even birds and other animals like squirrels and garden lizards will move away,” he added.
Mr. Reddy pointed out that the quality of life will also be impacted as temperature will take a hit. “With such a plethora of tree species, there will be multiple ecosystems and habitats that will also be destroyed,” he added.
Re-issue public notice
On September 20, the GBA issued a public notice inviting objections to the felling of trees, stating that details of the trees and their locations had been uploaded on the GBA website. However, three days later, the list has not been published.
Dattatraya Devare, an environmental activist, alleged that the GBA is handling the objection-inviting process negligently. “If they don’t upload the details, how can we specify our objections, and if it’s not specific, then the objection will be junked. They should re-issue the public notice after publishing the list and then re-invite objections,” he stated. Several other citizen groups have also raised the question, demanding the immediate uploading of details.
Petition against project
A petition opposing the proposed Hebbal Short Tunnel project has crossed 20,000 signatures, with citizens seeking an immediate pause to the project and independent assessments of its environmental, hydrological, traffic and safety impacts.
Launched on Change.org on August 3, the petition seeks to “Save Bengaluru’s Green-Blue Landscape” and raises concerns over the proposed ₹1,140-crore, 2.2-km cut-and-cover tunnel, which will likely pass through areas including the Hebbal lake buffer, Hebbal Tree Park, Veterinary College campus and UAS staff quarters.

stories.headline: Banks to deploy excess liquidity over next few months: RBI DG
stories.bodyText:
MUMBAI: 
RBI
 deputy governor Rohit Jain on Thursday said banks are expected to deploy additional liquidity from foreign currency non-resident deposits over the next few months, as credit demand is likely to be strong during the festive season.
Under the special Foreign Currency Non-Resident (FCNR-B) deposit scheme, banks have mobilised $133 billion. The scheme closed on Aug 31, one month ahead of the earlier schedule following a robust response from the Indian diaspora.
Talking to reporters on the sidelines of the SBI Banking & Economics Conclave here, Jain said RBI has held meetings with banks to discuss their liquidity position following the FCNR(B) inflows. "Banks are expected to deploy FCNR(B) liquidity over the next few months, helped by the upcoming festive season and strong credit demand," he said, adding that RBI is not directing banks to any particular sector to deploy the mobilised funds. Jain further said banks will have full discretion on deployment of FCNR(B) liquidity, based on their credit pipeline, proposals and liquidity outlook.
Banks' asset-liability position will determine how they use the additional liquidity, he added.
Jain said credit demand is broad-based, with all sectors and segments growing reasonably well, and the central bank does not see any particular sector requiring caution at present.

stories.headline: India can meet screen-protector demand locally, assures IT secy
stories.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India can manufacture enough smartphone screen protectors to meet its needs, IT secretary S Krishnan said, arguing that inferior imports should not erode the business of domestic producers investing in quality.
"We now have enough production capacity in the country for this category of equipment," Krishnan said on Thursday on the sidelines of an event in New Delhi.
His remarks underline the rationale behind govt's decision to place smartphone screen protectors under mandatory quality requirements. From April 1, 2027, the products will have to meet the applicable Indian Standard under the compulsory registration framework governing electronics and IT goods. Manufacturers and other entities covered by the requirement have until March 31 to prepare for compliance. Govt has cited public interest as the basis for extending the framework to this category.
Krishnan said keeping substandard products from being dumped in India was necessary to safeguard the market for locally manufactured, quality alternatives. With production capacity already available, his comments suggest the policy emphasis is shifting towards ensuring that domestic investment is not undermined by inferior competing products. 
The requirement could create an opportunity for companies building manufacturing operations in the segment.
For the industry, the transition will put greater emphasis on demonstrating conformity with the prescribed standard. However, the effect on retail prices, import volumes and domestic manufacturers' market shares remains to be seen.
Krishnan also pointed to firmer investment intent across electronics and semiconductors. "Last year, everyone had a sense of FOMO that they had to be here. This year they are actually making commitments," he said, describing discussions moving towards investment proposals, applications and expansion plans, alongside closer engagement between industry participants.

stories.headline: Tiruppur’s garment exports cross ₹46,000 crore in 2025-26

The exporters should leverage the opportunities coming through the free trade agreements, and adoption of technology should improve for Tiruppur to be competitive, he said.
Kumar Duraiswamy, joint secretary of the Association, said international buyers were looking at doubling the supplies from India to their countries by 2030.
N. Thirukkumaran, secretary of the Association, said that despite various challenges, knitwear exports from Tiruppur registered 2.49 % growth last fiscal over the previous year. Tiruppur contributes 54.74 % of knitwear exports from India. Under the Samarth scheme, nearly 19,050 people were trained in Tiruppur.
Mr. Subramanian launched a redesigned website of the association and awards were presented to 24 exporters for excellence in various categories.

stories.headline: Legal opinion ‘backs’ Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as Tata Sons chairman
stories.deck: While former Supreme Court judges Justice B.N. Srikrishna and Justice Uday U. Lalit opined the casting vote exercised by the chairman of the Tata Group board was valid under the company’s AoA
stories.bodyText:
Legal opinions obtained by Tata Sons support the validity of N. Chandrasekaran’s reappointment as chairman for a third five-year term, saying the provision in the company’s Articles of Association (AoA) that requires a Selection Committee applies to the appointment of a new chairman and not to the extension or reappointment of an incumbent.
While former Supreme Court judges Justice B.N. Srikrishna and Justice Uday U. Lalit opined the casting vote exercised by the chairman of the Tata Group board was valid under the company’s AoA, the September 17 board resolution giving Mr. Chandrasekaran a third term was on the lines of a similar one that gave him a second term in 2022.
Justice Srikrishna said the action was consistent with Article 121, while Justice Lalit said the equality of votes among directors appointed under Article 104B provided an occasion for the chairman to exercise a casting vote.
Tata Trusts, which owns about 66% of Tata Sons, challenged the September 17 board resolution giving Mr. Chandrasekaran a third term, arguing that its AoA requires affirmative support from a majority of Trust-nominated directors and a chairman’s casting vote cannot override that requirement.

briefs.headline: ‘Crude prices have risen 30% in a month’: CEA warns India exposed to multiple shocks
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Oil prices have shot up to $114 a barrel from below $85 in June and July, exposing India to multiple shocks as trade, technology and energy risks increasingly reinforce one another, chief economic adviser V Anantha Nageswaran said on Thursday.
Speaking at the SBI Banking and Economics Conclave, Nageswaran said India's imported crude basket had risen nearly 30% in Sept from Aug, while the price stood at $115.27 a barrel on Sept 22. "The effects on prices, capital, and trade end up amplifying each other," he said.
Nageswaran said supply shocks had become the dominant force shaping the global economy, with the pandemic, Ukraine war, trade restrictions, supply-chain disruptions, Persian Gulf conflict and the AI investment boom adding to pressures on production and prices.
He said the nature of the shocks had also changed, with countries increasingly using trade, technology and energy as strategic tools. "The worst shocks now arrive, not by accident, but by design," he said. "What India needs is resilience, not just self-reliance," he said, adding the country should aim for "diversified abundance".
India's decision to maintain strategic autonomy also carries a cost, he said. "India, given its geography and its size, cannot obviously belong to any bloc," Nageswaran said. 
"That sovereignty or that independence comes with its own cost, and we have to be prepared to pay that price."
He said India could face higher energy prices or more frequent supply disruptions as geopolitical blocs become more entrenched.
He said the global economy was moving away from the disinflationary conditions that prevailed from the 1990s to around 2020, when globalisation, trade integration and technology helped keep prices under control.
"We probably have put the disinflation era of the 1990 to 2015 or 2020 behind us right now. Commodity and real-asset prices are likely to remain under pressure as the global economy becomes more dependent on physical resources," he added.
Nageswaran said energy prices could remain elevated even if the current conflict is resolved because of rising demand from AI-related infrastructure. "The demand for energy in general coming from the AI model... will continue to keep pressure on energy prices in general on the higher side going forward," he said.
The higher cost of energy coincidentally comes at a time when countries are also competing more aggressively for capital.

briefs.headline: Rupee falls 26p to 95.99 against dollar amid crude oil spike

According to forex traders, the domestic currency was also weighed down by heavy selling in domestic equity markets as investors moved toward risk aversion, adding strength to the dollar, even as rising inflation concerns pushed US bond yields higher. briefs.headline: Insurance stocks crash as Irdai proposes tighter rules
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai: A host of insurance companies and insurance policy sellers slid as much as 36% on Thursday after the industry regulator Irdai suggested new policy distribution methods that, among others, ban dark patterns and several other changes to how insurance policies are sold that in turn could affect their revenue and bottom line.
Tech-driven insurance policy seller PolicyBazar crashed 36%, lost Rs 680 and closed at Rs 1,210, a 52-week low level on Thursday. Another company in the same line of business, TurtleMint, lost the maximum possible 20% and closed at the lower circuit at Rs 109. Among the pure-play insurance companies, HDFC Life crashed 6.1%, ICICI Prudential Life Insurance closed 4.2% down, LIC closed 0.3% while SBI Life closed just a tad higher, up 0.1%.
On Wednesday, Irdai proposed some changes to how insurance policies are sold and also how data relating to prospective insurance buyers are collected. It also proposed changes to expense of management limits and commission structures. Irdai also proposed some safeguards against mis-selling, a trait a large number of insurance buyers and people in general have complained about.
Irdai has proposed lowering limits for expense of management limits and also to put caps on commissions on various insurance products and distribution channels.
Some analysts and market players believe that such steps, on one hand, are pro-insurance buyers, but on the other, could severely dent revenues of some of the players. And hence the sell-off in their stocks on Thursday.
On a call in the evening, the management of PolicyBazar acknowledged that if these proposals are made into rules, there could be some meaningful impact on its business. However, they said that the market's reaction to its stock may have been on the higher side. It also said that the non-life business is expected to face a worse impact than the life business.

briefs.headline: Sebi allows FPIs in non-agri commodity derivatives trade
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: The board of market regulator Sebi on Thursday decided to allow foreign funds in the non-agri commodity derivatives segment provided all contracts that are not based on indices are cash settled. For index-based derivatives, there are no such barriers. Allowing foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) in this segment was one of the main demands of the commodity market players as well as foreign fund managers.
Sebi's board also said it would allow celebrity endorsements of Sebi-regulated products but with adequate safeguards.
In its board meeting, Sebi also said that very soon portfolio managers will be allowed to invest in foreign equities, including equities, debt, ETFs, REITs and mutual funds. Portfolio managers will be allowed to invest in unlisted debt securities and up to 1.25 times their clients' assets in exchange-traded derivatives. The regulator also said it will overhaul the settlement mechanism for violations of Sebi rules and introduce a new formula for calculating settlement amounts. It will fast-track the settlement mechanism for cases involving amounts of up to Rs 10 lakh.
Going ahead, there will be a single advertising code for stock brokers, mutual funds, investment advisers, portfolio managers and other Sebi-regulated entities.
Sebi's move to also allow foreign funds in the non-agri commodity derivatives space is aimed at increasing liquidity in the segment as the decision could bring in more institutional players. This could also improve the price discovery process in the space that in turn helps convergence between prices in the physical space and the derivatives segment. "With the objective of deepening liquidity in the commodity derivatives market, it's been decided...to permit participation of FPIs in the following contracts -- non-agricultural index derivatives contracts, irrespective of the underlying being cash-settled or not and non-cash-settled non-agricultural commodity derivatives contracts," a Sebi release said.
Sebi said that the new formula for calculating the settlement amount will be based on a base amount linked to the minimum penalty prescribed for the violation under securities laws. Under the new settlement mechanism, the terms for settlement will comprise the settlement amount, disgorgement of wrongful gains, and remedial and regulatory terms.

briefs.headline: NSE debuts on BSE with minor gains amid selloff
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Shares of National Stock Exchange (NSE), the largest bourse in India in terms of turnover and profit, listed on BSE at Rs 1,800, a marginal 0.8% premium to its IPO price of Rs 1,785 but rallied soon after. After touching an intraday high of 1,878, a 5% gain over its offer price, the stock closed at Rs 1,818, a 1.8% rise over its issue price.
At the close of Thursday's session, the bourse had a market capitalisation of Rs 4.5 lakh crore, which made it the 11th most valued company in India. NSE is now valued more than companies like Sun Pharma (Rs 4.4 lakh crore) and Titan (Rs 4.3 lakh crore) but less than Hindustan Unilever (Rs 4.5 lakh crore), LIC (Rs 5.1 lakh crore) and eight others.
On Sept 21, the exchange had closed its much-anticipated, yet much-delayed IPO, in which some of its existing shareholders together sold nearly 12.9 crore shares, raising Rs 22,568 crore. This made it the second biggest such offer in India, behind Hyundai India's Rs 28,900-crore offer that closed in Oct 2024. The issue was subscribed 5.7 times.
Current Sebi rules prohibit self-listing, meaning shares of an exchange or its subsidiaries can't be traded on its platform. So NSE was listed on BSE. On BSE, nearly 5.2 crore shares changed hands in NSE's debut session. Some of the large brokerages have given a buy recommendation for the stock. Among foreign brokerages, Macquarie started its coverage of the stock with an 'outperform' rating and a target price of Rs 1,965. Among the domestic ones, PL Capital initiated its coverage of NSE with an 'accumulate' rating and a target price of Rs 1,950.

briefs.headline: Rising yields, crude spike sink sensex
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: Rising global bond yields, a spike in crude oil prices and a weak overnight US market closing took a toll on Dalal Street on Thursday. As investors sold off, 
sensex
 closed 1,247 points or 1.7% down at 73,581 points, a more than three-month closing low. Financial stocks, which stand to be hit most by rising yields and hence interest rates, led the slide, along with index heavyweight Reliance Industries. On NSE, 
Nifty
 closed 384 points or 1.6% down at 23,063 points.
The day's selling was led by foreign funds, with the net outflow from stocks alone at Rs 5,027 crore, BSE data showed. Domestic funds, on the other hand, were net buyers at Rs 4,301 crore. The slide left investors poorer by about Rs 2.7 lakh crore, with India's market capitalisation now at Rs 482.3 lakh crore, data from BSE showed.
According to Vinod Nair of Geojit Investments, markets came under pressure amid rising bond yields and a rebound in crude oil prices, reflecting heightened global macroeconomic risks. "Investor sentiment turned increasingly risk averse as concerns over the interest rate trajectory intensified, driven by lingering uncertainties around inflation and economic growth. In the absence of fresh positive triggers, near-term sentiment may remain cautious, potentially limiting valuation expansion and making earnings growth likely to become the primary driver of market performance going forward.
"
Among sensex stocks, Reliance Industries, Axis Bank, Bajaj Finance, HDFC Bank and Bharti Airtel contributed the most to the index's loss on Thursday.
Of the 30 sensex stocks, 29 closed in the red. In the broader market, however, the advance-decline ratio was not as skewed in favour of the laggards. On BSE, 3,013 stocks closed lower compared to 1,362 that closed higher.

briefs.headline: Govt rules out MDR burden on UPI users; GST Council may review 18% tax next month
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: Govt on Thursday said the merchant discount rate (MDR) on UPI payments should be treated the same way as plastic payments, which are not passed on to consumers and will ask the Indian Bank Association (IBA) to ensure that merchants don't burden customers once the new regime kicks in next month. Govt is also hopeful that goods and services tax (GST) council will review the 18% tax levied on MDR on UPI and will take a "favourable" view as it affects common people.
The maximum retail price (MRP) of a product stays the same whether paid by debit card, UPI or credit card and merchants have always absorbed that MDR within MRP, a senior finance ministry official said.
All person-to-person UPI payments remain free, irrespective of the amount and all UPI merchant payments up to Rs 2,000 have no MDR levied. RuPay debit card transactions also continue to have zero MDR. "Why should UPI be treated any differently? Govt is not going to get a single rupee. It is not a cess or surcharge, neither a tax. The whole MDR amount will remain within the payment ecosystem and will be shared among banks and other entities," the official added.
Though no advisory has yet been given to IBA, govt will be holding talks with the association to ensure that a mechanism is in place to not burden the consumer. 
"IBA needs to hold awareness campaigns and outreach programmes, preferably in regional and local languages," the official said.
The official added that MDR is not unique to India and payment systems globally levy 1.5-3% charge on credit cards and UPI systems. "The cost of running the entire ecosystem may still not be recovered by this. NPCI may still have to depend on govt support," the official said.
Backing the decision, the official said MDR is being levied on select high-value transactions to make India's indigenous UPI ecosystem financially sustainable over long-term. This will help fund servers, payment infrastructure, cybersecurity, fraud detection and improve and expand UPI to feature phones as well. "There are nearly 56 crore UPI users, leaving substantial room for expansion, especially in rural and semi-urban areas," the official said.
Fears around the increase in cash usage after the rollout are also misplaced and govt is ready to engage with trader bodies as well. "The aim is to create awareness at all levels," the official added.

briefs.headline: UPI transactions costing banks about 21k cr annually, says NPCI CEO Asbe
briefs.bodyText: MUMBAI: UPI's new merchant fee is intended to recover some of the cost that the payments system has so far absorbed. Dilip Asbe, MD & CEO of NPCI, put the annual cost to the banking system at about Rs 21,000 crore, including Rs 2,000 crore to Rs 3,000 crore for SBI. In a fireside chat with SBI DMD Chander Shekhar Sharma at the SBI Banking and Economic Conclave, the NPCI chief said that the costs of technology have risen, with servers which cost Rs 20 lakh last year now costing Rs 1 crore. He added that NPCI has exhausted most of its technology budget having met only a fourth of its requirements. Bankers say that besides the load on the core banking and storage systems, every account-to-account transfer requires banks to send out alert messages for every transaction. TNN

stories.headline: Asian Games: Diya-Manush assure India of Asian Games table tennis medal
stories.bodyText:
Joshana Chinappa has another Asian Games medal, 16 years after winning her first.
The 40-year-old, partnering Velavan Senthilkumar, stormed into the mixed doubles squash semifinals with a straight-game win over their Filipino opponents, 11-3, 11-5.
The victory assures India of at least a bronze medal in the event.
Joshana and Velavan will face Hong Kong's Lee Ka Yi and Tang Ming Hong in the semifinals tomorrow.
Joshana Chinappa and Velavan Senthilkumar have made a flying start to their mixed doubles squash quarterfinal against their Filipino opponents.
The Indian pair have blitzed through the opening game, winning it 11-3.
A table tennis medal at the Asian Games for India!
Diya Chitale and Manush Shah have stormed into the mixed doubles semifinals after knocking out Hong Kong's world No. 4 pair Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem in the quarterfinals.
The Indian pair, ranked eighth in the world, won 3-1 (11-6, 13-15, 11-9, 11-5) to assure India of only their second Asian Games medal in mixed doubles table tennis.
That's the end of Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade's mixed doubles campaign at the Asian Games.
The Indian pair went down 0-3 to China's Lin Shidong and Kuai Man in the quarterfinal, losing 5-11, 10-12, 9-11.
Diya Chitale and Manush Shah are just one game away from securing a mixed doubles table tennis medal after taking a 2-1 lead over Hong Kong's Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem.
The Hong Kong pair fought back to win the third game, but the Indian duo remain in front in this crucial quarterfinal.
INDIA QUALIFY FOR THE FINAL! Kamaljeet and Suruchi have delivered an outstanding performance in the mixed team 10m air pistol qualification, finishing with 587 to top the standings.
The Indian pair produced three superb series of 196, 195 and 196, finishing just four points short of the world record.
It is a huge turnaround after the struggles of the last two days, with Kamaljeet and Suruchi now through to the final as qualification toppers.
Iran, South Korea and Indonesia will join India in the final. The qualification scores will not carry over, with all four pairs starting from scratch.
Diya Chitale and Manush Shah have made a strong start in their mixed doubles quarterfinal against Hong Kong's Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem, taking the opening game 11-6.
It is a crucial start in what could be a medal-deciding contest for the Indian pair.
Meanwhile, Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade have dropped the first game against China's Lin Shidong and Kuai Man.
India have two pairs in action in the mixed doubles quarterfinals, with both ties carrying medal significance.
Diya Chitale and Manush Shah take on Hong Kong's Wong Chun Ting and Doo Hoi Kem.
Harmeet Desai and Yashaswini Ghorpade face China's Lin Shidong and Kuai Man.
Both Indian pairs need a win to book their places in the semifinals.
Kamaljeet and Suruchi continue to impress in the mixed team 10m air pistol qualification, with India adding 195 in their second series of 20 shots.
After a 196 in the opening series, India have now moved to 391 with just 20 shots remaining. They are currently sitting at the top of the standings, with a place in the final within sight.
The top four pairs will advance to the final, as Kamaljeet and Suruchi look to keep India's medal hopes alive in the event.
India's Pooja has registered a 5.18m jump in her first attempt of the women's heptathlon long jump, scoring 609 points.
She was not pleased with the effort and will have two more attempts to improve her mark.
Kamaljeet and Suruchi have made a superb start in the mixed team 10m air pistol qualification, firing 196 in their first 20 shots to sit at the top of the standings for now.
This is India's final chance for a medal in the 10m air pistol events after a disappointing campaign so far. Kamaljeet finished ninth in the individual qualification, while Suruchi was 26th, with neither making the individual final. India also missed out on medals in both the men's and women's team events.
The top four pairs from qualification will advance to the final.

The Indian pair made a dominant start, comfortably taking the opening game 21-8.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: I was encouraged to quit, but here I am, says Joshna
briefs.deck: The forty-year-old is competing at the Asian Games for a remarkable seventh time; the veteran, still chasing gold, is keen to add to her tally of five medals at the quadrennial showpiece
briefs.bodyText:
For nearly a quarter of a century, Joshna Chinappa has stood like a colossus on the squash court. At 40, Joshna doesn’t seem to have lost her fighting spirit and tenacity.
She knows she is ageing, has tweaked her training module accordingly and has remained one of the finest players in the country a good 24 years after she made her Asian Games debut in Busan in 2002.
Taking part only in the women’s team and mixed doubles (with Velavan Senthilkumar) events at the ongoing Aichi-Nagoya Games, the veteran from Chennai is more than eager to bag another medal.
Seeded third in mixed doubles, the Velavan-Joshna duo will take on the fellow Indian pair of Suraj Chand and Shameena Riaz in the round of 16 after having received a bye in the first. In the women’s team event (Anahat Singh, Tanvi Khanna and Shameena are her teammates), the No. 3-seeded India has been drawn in Pool C alongside Japan, China and Iran.
On the PSA World Tour, Joshna’s career has overlapped with three generations of elite squash players. Most of her contemporaries — Nicol David (43), Laura Massaro (42), Jenny Duncalf (43), Alison Waters (42) and Annie Au (37) — have long retired, underlining her remarkable longevity.
Placed 73rd in the chart, Joshna is India’s third-highest ranked woman behind the 18-year-old Anahat Singh (World No. 17) and Tanvi Khanna (World No. 71). A winner of 11 PSA titles, she continues to perform at a high level and is determined to make another significant contribution at the Asian Games. Everyone who has followed Joshna’s career knows how meticulous and disciplined she is in her preparation.
Saurav Ghosal, a former men’s top-10 player, perhaps perfectly summed up her longevity. “First and foremost, she really, really loves the game. She’s immensely talented, but she has also worked tirelessly on every aspect of her game to remain at the top for as long as she has. I hope that she comes back from the Asian Games with quite a few gold medals.”
In this interview with The Hindu, the five-time Asian Games medallist reflects on her longevity, debut at the 2002 Asiad, most cherished memories from the continental showpiece, and the motivation that continues to drive her at the highest level. Excerpts:
You are competing at the Asian Games for the seventh time, becoming the first Indian sportsperson to achieve the feat...
I honestly didn’t think I would make a seventh Asian Games appearance. I just focused on my training and tournaments. It definitely feels great to be a part of the Indian team again.
You have won five medals at the Asiad, but a gold remains elusive. What are the chances of clinching the yellow metal?
We have a strong team and yes, it would be great to win another medal. I have always taken my matches one at a time, so I am as prepared as I can be.
Looking back, which was your best Asian Games?
Performance-wise, 2018 would probably be the best I played (singles bronze and silver in women’s team).
How special was it to be on the Asiad stage as a teenager?
As a 15-year-old, it was amazing to see so many superstars of Indian sport in one Village. There is one memory that stands out from my first Games in Busan in 2002. We are usually given our official India clothing and I would obviously wear that to play and train. But in my down time at the Village, I wore a personal T-shirt at the food hall a couple of times, and legendary hockey player Dhanraj Pillay told me that I had to be in my India clothing. It’s something we should always be proud of. It was inspiring for me because it made me aware that I am always representing my country at the Games on and off court... that has stayed with me till now.
You were part of the top 10 in the PSA rankings thrice. When you got there for the first time as a 29-year-old in July 2016, how did you feel?
The top 10 is a special place. It took a lot of effort, especially coming back from my ACL surgery, and years of work with my team.
There were top players like Nour El Sherbini, Raneem El Welily, Nouran Gohar, Camille Serme and Massaro. So how difficult was it to get or stay there?
I definitely played with a bunch of incredibly talented and hardworking women who were greats of the game. Playing with them, beating some of them and making it to the top 10 was one of the best moments of my career.
What did the win over Nicol — an eight-time World champion — in the 2018 Asian Games women’s team semifinals mean to you?
It meant a lot because I have always looked up to her and admired how humble she is as a champion. I really wanted to do it for the team. She is one of the greatest of all-time. Coming in from the disappointment of losing singles and making the team final after beating a strong team like Malaysia was amazing!
You had a on-court rivalry with Dipika Pallikal but shared a bond and went on to bag medals at the Asian Games and Commonwealth Games...
We have had some amazing wins together for India and I will always think of my time competing with her and playing alongside her as inspiring and motivating.
You have won 11 Tour titles. You had to wait 10 years to earn your latest crown, at the Japan Open in 2025. Why did it take so long to end the drought?
I didn’t expect to win in Japan. It felt great to win after ages, especially since I beat girls who were in their early 20s and were ranked way higher than me. The difference now is that I am a lot more relaxed towards competing and I am more performance-oriented than result-focused. Maybe it just helps me enjoy and appreciate these moments more and play better squash.
Every title I have won has come at different times of my life: they all have come after years of training and preparation. Each one has been rewarding.
How have you been able to sustain at this level for nearly quarter of a century? Is it down to mental sharpness, your focus on fitness, outlook towards life or all three?
The main reason I am able to still compete today is my parents. My team, including my coach, strength and conditioning trainer, physios, nutritionist and sports psychologist, has been amazing. The support from my sponsors, the State government, Central government and Squash Rackets Federation of India has been great. It takes a lot to compete at the highest level and it’s only possible because of the amazing people I work with. I do work a lot on the mental and physical side of the game besides recovery. I really appreciate and worship my body, which has been so incredibly supportive.
How much has the sport evolved since you began playing?
So much! At the international level, the game has become so much more physically demanding, faster and skilful. Domestically, we have many players playing, and the level has improved a lot. Seeing so many PSA (World Tour) events happening in India is wonderful because many of our players benefit tremendously by playing in them and watching the top players competing here in India.
Squash will make its debut at the 2028 LA Olympics...
Such exciting times ahead for squash. India has a great chance to do well.
You had knee injuries/surgeries in 2011 and 2023? How challenging was it physically and mentally to come back from those?
I tore my ACL on the right knee in 2011 and was out of the game for a year. I was encouraged to quit playing and get into coaching. I had no financial support but I moved to Bombay (Mumbai) and worked with a really good Egyptian physio and trainer — Ahmed Youssef. When I got back to playing, coach Ritwik Bhattacharya helped me. Some of my best victories came after that surgery because I believed I had a lot more to offer to the game and I really wanted to play for India again.
And in 2023, during the last Asian Games, I found that there was no cartilage in my right knee and it also needed a surgery. But I did the surgery more for quality of life as it was painful to do basic things like driving, getting out of bed comfortably and jogging. My surgeon, Dr. Jagdeesh, who did my ACL surgery, also did my cartilage surgery and told me that I would be able to compete again. So I moved to Bengaluru and worked with Yash Pandey at Peak Performance. I got back on court after five months of rehab. I decided to train and play for a couple more years to see if I could play the Asian Games.
How big a support has your father been and what are your memories of playing with him at Madras Cricket Club?
My dad is the main reason I am here today. He introduced me to the game as he was a squash player himself. I have the best memories of tagging along with him to the MCC and playing squash with him, other MCC members and my friends. He was my coach and motivator for a very long time, especially when I was a junior.

briefs.headline: Agarkar’s roller-coaster ride
briefs.deck: When the former pacer was named the chairman of selectors in July 2023, there was a sense of great optimism and feel-good; his tenure, however, was a chequered one with highs in the white-ball format and lows in the Tests
briefs.bodyText:
From all indications, BCCI senior chief selector Ajit Agarkar has chaired his last selection committee meeting. A little over a week back, the Agarkar-led panel picked the national squads to do duty against West Indies in three One-Day Internationals and five Twenty20 Internationals, apart from naming the Rest of India side to take on Ranji Trophy champions Jammu & Kashmir in the Irani Cup.
Among those named in the ODI squad was Rohit Sharma, the former captain whose future has been needlessly put under the microscope over the last 12 months. It is widely perceived that Rohit has inadvertently become the primary reason for Agarkar choosing, as is being touted, not to seek an extension to his term as chairman of selectors when his tenure ends early next week.
Good rapport
When Agarkar was named the chairman in July 2023, there was a sense of great optimism and feel-good. He had played alongside Rohit, by then firmly entrenched as the all-format skipper, as well as head coach Rahul Dravid. He shared a good rapport with the two men that formed the core leadership group, and it was widely anticipated that this troika would work in tandem to push Indian cricket further ahead on the path to dominance.
The honeymoon period lasted for a fair while, it can’t be disputed. Under Rohit, India charged through to the final of the home 50-over World Cup in 2023 before coming a cropper in the title round against Australia, then mounted a flawless, unbeaten campaign in the Americas as they won a second T20 World Cup crown in Bridgetown in June 2024. In some ways, that victory was to prove a decisive moment in Indian cricket, and not necessarily for the reasons one might consider organic or positive.
Dravid’s tenure as head coach ended with India’s defeat to Australia, before he was persuaded by the Board of Control for Cricket in India and, more decisively, by a phone call from Rohit, to stay on till the end of the T20 World Cup. That proved to be a masterstroke; Rohit and Dravid realised there was unfinished business to address, and while the T20 World Cup might not hold the same aura as its more established white-ball counterpart, it was immensely satisfying for the two driven men that, finally, they had worthwhile silverware to show for their hegemony, hard work and entertaining, aggressive brand of cricket.
As Dravid walked away into the sunset and V.V.S. Laxman expressed his inability to take over as head coach, the BCCI’s hunt for a successor to the Bengalurean ended with Gautam Gambhir, the pugnacious former opener with a feisty, confrontational streak. Gambhir came with his own set of ideas. Unstated but perhaps somewhere near the top of that list was a desire to put together a new, young Test team that didn’t have a place at some stage in the not-too-distant future for Rohit, his predecessor Virat Kohli and off-spinning giant R. Ashwin.
The first seeds of discontent were sowed in Gambhir’s second series in charge, at home against New Zealand in October-November 2024. India were crushed 0-3, their first home series loss in more than a decade, and the finger-pointing began almost immediately.
Within months of that debacle, the celebrated trio had played its last Tests at different times on the subsequent tour of Australia, which India lost 1-3. Rohit missed the first game, victory in Perth, as he was away on paternity leave, and when he rejoined the team, his form deserted him summarily. Ashwin retired midway through the series, Rohit dropped himself for the final game in Sydney owing to poor form and Kohli’s tour unravelled dramatically after an unbeaten second-innings hundred in Perth as he unerringly found the slip cordon time after time.
Tricky path to transition
Rohit and Kohli announced their retirement from Test cricket within a week of each other in May 2025. By this time, Gambhir and Agarkar had already embarked on the tricky path to transition. To lose three giants in one fell swoop isn’t easy to recover from. Agarkar’s panel had its work cut out but it showed gumption and a propensity to go with its gut by naming Shubman Gill as the Test captain.
Gill’s first assignment was an away tour of England, where he showed sensational form and reasonably promising tactical awareness in securing a fabulous 2-2 stalemate. The captain led from the front with four hundreds, including a monumental 269 in Birmingham, on his way to 754 dazzling runs and eked out fantastic returns from Mohammed Siraj and Prasidh Krishna as both of India’s victories came when Jasprit Bumrah was rested to manage his workload.
Agarkar’s panel bared its intentions when it brought Gill back into the T20I setup —– as the vice-captain to Suryakumar Yadav, no less — and thrust him into the hot-seat in the ODI format too last October. Between the Australia Test series and IPL 2025, during the course of which Rohit and Kohli announced their Test retirements, India had won five matches on the trot to storm to the Champions Trophy title in the desert sands of Dubai in March.
Rohit had masterminded that charge with aplomb, using his bat as a scything weapon and leading with characteristic nous and acumen, but in a clear indication that he was on borrowed time, Agarkar and his men believed a change in leadership was imperative with the next 50-over World Cup two years away.
Steadfast, dignified silence
From that point, Rohit has been a marked man, his every move dissected, his every ODI series touted as his international swansong. All of a sudden, from being the most important man in Indian cricket, he was put in a difficult place, almost having to ‘prove’ himself time after time. To his credit, the Mumbaikar has maintained a steadfast, dignified silence — much like he did when he was summarily divested of the Mumbai Indians captaincy a couple of years back even though he had led the franchise to five titles — and allowed his bat to do the talking.
The last straw, the consensus is, in the Agarkar vs. Rohit saga — a saga unfolding in social media and on the internet and in reams of newsprint — came in England in July. Ostensibly, Rohit had been asked to announce his retirement at the end of the three-match series, after the final game at Lord’s. In the lead-up to the last ODI, epitaphs were being written, cryptic posts appeared on social media platforms and it was more or less accepted that Rohit wouldn’t play for the country again, until, in an unprecedented move, BCCI secretary Devajit Saikia voluntarily declared that Lord’s would not be Rohit’s swansong.
Clearly, that hasn’t gone down well with Agarkar, and understandably so. Selection matters are the prerogative of the selectors, specifically appointed for that sole purpose. If the BCCI wanted Rohit to continue, the secretary or the office-bearers could have had a word in private with Agarkar to express their stance. The public declaration, without provocation, raised Agarkar’s hackles and his relationship with the BCCI, it is presumed, soured from that point in mid-July onwards.
Notwithstanding the unseemly haste in trying to get rid of one of the greatest white-ball practitioners of all time, Agarkar had reason to feel miffed, if not downright insulted. But he didn’t cover himself in glory by not attending the review meeting called by the BCCI in Mumbai at the beginning of this month. By now, it was evident that things had reached a point of no-return, and even though Saikia made a spirited defence of the Agarkar no-show by citing personal reasons, no one had any doubts that the die had been cast.
If Agarkar does bow out, his report card will be a mixed bag. During his 38-month tenure, India won two T20 World Cups, two Asia Cups (one each in the 50- and the 20-over formats) and made it to the final of the 50-over World Cup at home. But their Test record has been abysmal – home series routs by New Zealand and South Africa (2-0 last November), and an away series loss to Australia in 2024-25 (1-3) completely cancel out all else, including a 1-0 victory in Sri Lanka last month.
Left-field decision
India have stuttered and stumbled in the transition phase, especially when it comes to bowling, and there has been a certain ambivalence in white-ball selection. The return of Shreyas Iyer to the T20I ecosystem after three years, in the role of captain, is as much of a left-field decision as the hasty call-up and dumping of Gill from the same version last year. From the days when Indian squads looked settled and were fuelled by consistency in selection, there is a sense of insecurity and of nervously looking over one’s shoulder, which is fair from the ideal scenario in which anyone can give off their best.
There have been reports of a breakdown in communication between Agarkar and Laxman, the head of the Centre of Excellence, especially when it comes to picking India ‘A’ squads. The CoE has chalked out long-standing pathways to prepare the next set of emerging talent for international cricket, but the selection panel has often chosen to override that pathway and thrust established Indian Test players into the mix, ostensibly for match practice, even in familiar home conditions. It is reliably learnt that Laxman wasn’t even consulted when the selectors picked the squad for the Asian Games though it was clear many months back that he would be the coach in Aichi-Nagoya. So much for transparency and openness isn’t a quip without substance.
Should events unfold along expected lines, India will have a new chairman very soon. They must too, because the squads for the tour of New Zealand, beginning with the first of five T20Is in Christchurch on October 22, need to be picked; the team is expected to depart from Bengaluru on October 18. The T20Is will be followed by five ODIs, the first phase of the final leg of preparations for the World Cup, and two Tests. Whoever the new chairman is — for now, the needle points in the direction of former India stumper Parthiv Patel, who led unfancied Gujarat to the Ranji Trophy title in January 2017 — will first have to ensure an equanimous relationship with the two captains and the head coach to ensure that the winds of uncertainty threatening to sweep through the cricketing landscape are calmed, if not quelled, post haste.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Persistence and drama as India’s mixed relay team, Seema win medals
briefs.deck: The 4x400m quartet of Vishal, Poovamma, Manu and Vithya earns silver while Seema, competing in her maiden Asiad, takes home bronze in 10,000m
briefs.bodyText:
Thirty minutes of persistence on the track followed by three of absolute drama saw day one of track and field competition end with a bronze and silver for India as the country opened its Asian Games athletics medal tally in Nagoya on Thursday (September 24, 2026).
Also read | Greco-Roman wrestler Deepak seeks urgent hearing in bid to make Asian Games squad
The 4x400m mixed relay team rode on tactical personnel changes, impressive lead-off and anchor legs and a stroke of luck to finish in 3:14.46, earning silver in the final event of the day at the Paloma Mizuho stadium. Minutes before, Seema had ended a 16-year drought in 10,000m, willing herself past the line in 32:50.05 to come third.
The Indian quartet of Vishal T.K. — India’s only sub-45-second quartermiler — M.R. Poovamma, Manu T.S. and Vithya Ramraj played their roles to perfection. Vishal ran with blistering pace before Poovamma and Manu ensured the team did not fall too far behind. Vithya, the only surviving member of the team that won silver in 2023, kicked in an extra gear, edging past Vietnam by a mere 0.08 seconds.
Interestingly, India was second in its heat in the morning, clocking 3:16.23, but replaced Jay Kumar and Kiran with Vishal and Vithya for the final.
The UAE, which had led for a large part of the race, fumbled towards the end, with Mariam Kareem dropping the baton just before the final lap. She did try to retrieve it and complete but the team was disqualified by the officials. Even though the UAE protested, the result stayed. Bahrain, led by the indefatigable Salwa Eid Naser, retained top spot with a new Games record of 3:12.87.
Seema wins 10,000m bronze
Seema, meanwhile, became only the third Indian woman to medal in the 10,000m at the Asian Games, after Preeja Sreedharan and Kavita Raut’s historic gold-silver double back in 2010. The 25-year-old, competing in her first Asiad, was impressive as much in her endurance to keep pace with the lead group — which included the likes of Yavi Winfred, Ruth Jebet and local star Nozomi Tanaka — as her race intelligence.
“I led for the first couple of laps and then realised that no one was going to [take the] lead because the best runners will always wait for the final laps. I changed my strategy and decided to run like others because this is my first competition at this level,” Seema said.
“At one point, I thought I could go for the win, but I could not push as hard as the others did. But now I have begun to understand the tactics and race strategy. The next time, I will not wait so long to push myself. I will use my learning from here in the 5000m,” she added.
Heartbreak in triple jump; sprinters reach semis
Triple jumper Asha Ilango suffered a heartbreak, coming fourth despite a best of 13.83m — it was the same as Li Yi of China but the Indian missed out on countback.
Li, the reigning Asian champion, had 13.79m as her next best jump while Asha had 13.65m. Niharika Vashisht finished 10th with a best effort of 13m. Uzbekistan’s Sharifa Davronova defended her title with a massive 14.35m, with Huang Yingying of China second with 14.12m.
Both Animesh Kujur and Gurindervir Singh advanced to the semifinals from their respective 100m heats. Anamika A.K. was seventh in heptathlon after four events with 3177 points and Pooja was ninth with 3159 points.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad: Savitha saves the day for Indian women; open team held
briefs.bodyText:
A late equaliser from B. Savitha Shri helped the Indian women draw with Kazakhstan in the Chess Olympiad on Thursday. The men’s team also was held to a draw by Azerbaijan at Samarkand.
With the tournament in its business-end, it indeed was not ideal for India, the defending champion in both the sections. It could, of course, have been much worse if Savitha hadn’t been able to pull off that hard-fought win against Elnaz Kaliakhmet.
The 19-year-old from Chennai has been having a dream Olympiad debut in Uzbekistan. She has won all her seven games and is well poised to win an individual medal regardless of how her team fares. She was in a must-win situation on this day, as India was trailing 1-2, thanks to R. Vaishali’s loss to Alua Nurman on the second board. Koneru Humpy and Divya Deshmukh had drawn their games.
It was a drawn rook-pawn ending, but once Kaliakhmet erred, Savitha ensured she converted the advantage and won in 62 moves. That earned India a precious match point and now has 13 points, two less than the sole leader China. On 14 points are Kazakhstan, Armenia and Mongolia.
In the open section, India is in the joint second position with 13 points, one behind the leaders Uzbekistan and Germany.
All the Indian players drew with their Azerbaijan rivals.
The day’s biggest upset was provided by Germany, which won 2.5-1.5 against Uzbekistan to open up the race to the top spot. Only three more rounds remain.

briefs.headline: Asian Games 2026: Satnam and Salman win a historic bronze
briefs.deck: The two were also the only Indian rowers to win a medal in this edition
briefs.bodyText:
At the end of the men’s double sculls event at the 2026 Asian Games, Salman Khan had his burly hand held up by a volunteer as he navigated the short, 10-foot ramp out of the water on trembling legs.
Satnam Singh couldn’t even do that.
They completed the race in 6:13.25s, just under three seconds behind second-placed Uzbekistan pair of Mekhrojbek Mamatkulov and Pavel Sorin. China’s Yi Xudi, Nie Yide (6:09.77) won the gold.
Even as he lay on his back, Satnam cried out: “Gold chala gaya (we lost the gold).”
As uncharitable as they were to themselves, the two had still made history. Not only were they the first Indian duo to achieve a podium finish in this event in the Games history, they were also the only Indian rowers to win a medal in Nagoya.
It’s almost a miracle that they did.
They were meant to take part in the men’s quadruple sculls, considered the marquee event.
Then, two days before the start of their competition, the rowing federation decided to split up India’s settled pairings. Satnam and Salman were moved to the double sculls, an event they had never competed in together.
“Sab nirash ho gaye the (we were depressed). The hardest part was we were removed from quad and placed into doubles. We didn’t eat or drink or sleep that night,” recalled Salman.
They protested. They considered quitting. Eventually, they decided to do what they needed to.
“What matters most is desh ka naam aur nishan (the country’s name and flag). We have to keep it high. Whatever happens later happens later,” Salman said.
With next to no preparation, they took to the course on Thursday morning armed with little more than willpower.
“Bas power se chali ye boat (the boat moved on power alone),” said Salman.
Incredibly, for the first half-kilometre, they were even in second place.
Then the Uzbeks pair came back strongly at the end, finishing just ahead of the Indians. But with their final strokes, Salman and Satnam kept going, eventually crossing the line just ahead of Indonesia.

briefs.headline: Horse declared ‘unfit’ by EFI gets all-clear from Asian Games organisers
briefs.deck: Chheda’s 19-year-old horse, Dono Di Maggio, cleared the mandatory veterinary inspection ahead of Friday’s dressage competition, directly clearing the way for the rider to compete.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: A horse declared “unfit” by the Equestrian Federation of India’s (EFI) ad-hoc committee in Germany has now been declared fit by Asian Games organisers in Japan, putting the spotlight on the veterinary assessment process used to determine Hriday Chheda’s participation in the continental event.
Chheda’s 19-year-old horse, Dono Di Maggio, cleared the mandatory veterinary inspection ahead of Friday’s dressage competition, directly clearing the way for the rider to compete. The contrasting findings have left Chheda questioning why Dono was declared unfit in Aachen and whether the assessment ordered by the ad-hoc committee was fair.
“My horse is perfectly fit and healthy as checked in the mandatory vet inspection by the organisers. This has been a relief. I’d like to thank Indian Olympic Association (IOA) president PT Usha for supporting me and ensuring that I get my fair chance to compete here. I’m looking forward to winning a medal for India,” Chheda told TOI from Tokyo.
Riders draw up own start order
Meanwhile, another selection dispute has surfaced in the dressage squad. TOI has learnt that three riders — Gaurav Pundir, Chheda and Shruti Vora — have rejected the start order proposed by the ad-hoc committee for Friday’s competition and formally submitted their own sequence to the panel and India’s chef-de-mission Sahdev Yadav.
In their mail, the riders said the order should be based on “objective merit, experience, recent results and scores”. They proposed that the youngest and least experienced rider, Jai Sud, go first. Their suggested order is: Jai Sud, Hriday Chheda/Gaurav Pundir, Gaurav Pundir/Hriday Chheda and Shruti Vora.
The riders pointed out that Sud began competing internationally only in March 2026 and has no previous championship experience at this level. Chheda was part of India’s 2023 Hangzhou Games gold-medal winning team, Pundir was part of India’s 2025 Asian Continental Championships silver-medal winning team, while senior rider Vora is a triple silver medallist from the same event.

briefs.headline: Chess Olympiad R8: India miss chance to close in as Gukesh draws
briefs.deck: Gukesh pushed hard but was held to a draw by Azerbaijan’s Mahammad Muradli as India missed a chance to close the gap on the Chess Olympiad leaders. Uzbekistan and Germany lead the open section with 14 points. In the women’s event, Savitha Shri extended her winning streak to seven, rescuing India against Kazakhstan and keeping their title hopes alive.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: India had a smooth sail in the open section of the 2026 Chess Olympiad until their Round 6 game against hosts Uzbekistan in Samarkand. We all know what happened there.
With the other three boards drawn, Nihal Sarin had an advantage against Nodirbek Yakubboev, only to blunder his queen, the match slipped from India's grip, handing Uzbekistan the lead in the title race. While Sarin's blunder dominated the post-match discussion in chess circles, some also asked whether world champion Dommaraju Gukesh could have pushed his own game a little further instead of settling for a draw.
Vidit Gujrathi, briefly joining ChessBase India's commentary panel on his rest day, brushed the suggestion aside. "Gukesh plays his own game," he said. "If he feels there is a chance, he pushes till the very end." India needed exactly that in the Round 8 match-up against Azerbaijan's Mahammad Muradli.
With the other three boards ending in draws, Gukesh needed a win to settle the match and keep India's title defence alive, a defence that had looked bleak even a day earlier.
As Germany beat Uzbekistan at the other end of the hall on Thursday, a win for Gukesh would have put India within touching distance of the new leaders. He pushed for one, right until the position simplified into a draw he couldn't avoid.
Playing white in a Najdorf Sicilian, Gukesh went for the ambitious 7.Qf3, and Muradli responded accurately with 7...h6 and some active queen manoeuvres. Both sides simplified quickly in the early middlegame, with 16.Bxc4 Qxc4 17.Qd3 Qxd3 leading into a queenless position. Gukesh carved out some queenside space with 27.b4 and 28.b5, while Muradli locked down the centre and activated his king in response.
The game turned into a fierce time-pressure battle from there.
By move 35, both players had under two minutes each, but Gukesh kept the position balanced. Even after the time control, the resulting rook-and-bishop ending proved impossible to crack — Muradli's active rook checks, starting with 48...Rb2+, forced Gukesh's king into a repeating sequence, and neither side could make further progress.
The players shook hands on a draw after 56...Rb2+, a resilient defensive display from Muradli against sustained pressure from the world champion.
As things stand, Uzbekistan and Germany lead the standings with 14 points apiece. A chasing pack on 13 includes China, Azerbaijan, the United States, India, Armenia and France, with all hoping for further slip-ups at the top that they can pounce on.
Savitha Shri saves Indian women's day again
Savitha Shri's dominant run on Board 4 continued into Thursday, stretching her winning streak to seven as India's women held Kazakhstan to a 2-2 draw. It was Savitha, once again, who came to her side's rescue after the team fell behind when Alua Nurman beat Vaishali Rameshbabu on Board 2.
With Divya Deshmukh and Koneru Humpy having already drawn their games against Meruert Kamalidenova and Bibisara Assaubayeva, respectively, India needed a win on Board 4 to stay in the title hunt, and Savitha delivered.
It was a hard-fought battle against Elnaz Kaliakhmet, played out through an Italian Game (Giuoco Piano) that turned into a long strategic grind. After the quiet opening moves, 1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4 d6, both sides manoeuvred patiently before the middlegame tension picked up.
Savitha's unusual 11.Ra4 and the rook manoeuvres that followed showed a willingness to play the long game, and the position tipped in her favour after 25.Nf5 gave White a more comfortable structure. Queens came off soon after, leading into a demanding rook-and-pawn endgame.
With both players deep into time trouble, Savitha's technique held up under pressure. Moves like 52.Rd5+ and 54.dxe4 kept her ahead practically, while 59.Rxd3 simplified the position into a winning king-and-rook ending. Kaliakhmet resigned after 62.Ra2.
